Hon. J. D. HAZEN (Minister of Marine and Fisheries) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 75, to amend the Canada Shipping Act. He said: The introduction of this Bill as considered necessary in consequence of the very extensive use of gasolene and oil engines in boats in Canada. Under the present law, any boat that is over fiv'e tons in size and carries passengers is required to have a certificated engineer .and a certificated captain. There are a laTge number of .motor boats over five tons that are being used for passenger service in Canada at the present time and"! am advised by the technical officers of the department that it is not necessary for the safety of the public that these boats should be compelled to carry both a certificated engineer and a certificated master. There is a provision in the law at present that no person shall act in the double capacity of

master and engineer of any steamboat. It is proposed to amend the section, so far as regards boats that do not exceed sixty-five feet in length, and provide, under regulations to be made by the department, that it will be sufficient to have one man who is both a certificated engineer and a certificated captain. Any man who possesses both certificates will be allowed to command the boat, and also to act as engineer. The present Act makes provision for engineers' certificates in the case of boats driven by steam only, and it is proposed to make some changes so that a special certificate may he granted to an engineer in charge of a boat driven by a gasolene, oil or combustion engine.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

Mr. Speaker, in the
course of the debate upon the motion by the right hon. leader of the Opposition for an investigation into the operations of the Shell Committee, I used the following language :
Now, what course does the Government propose to take with regard to the motion which my right hon. friend has proposed to this House? As far as the Shell Committee is concerned-I shall speak afterwards of another matter-our proposal is this. We shall direct the attention of the British Government in detail to every charge, allegation and rumour brought up in this house or elsewhere by my right hon. friend, or by any of his supporters with regard to the Shell Committee. We shall further inform the British Government that if an inquiry is thought advisable, we are prepared to co-operate with them to the fullest extent, and to issue any commission, take any proceedings, pass any legislation, and do any other act for the purpose of making that inquiry as full, thorough, and complete as they deem advisable. But without their consent or approval, we do not propose to enter upon an investigation or inquiry into such expenditures by the British Government.
And further on I spoke as follows:
If, however, he or any of his followers has a charge to make against any member of the Government with respect to the Shell Committee, or with respect to anything else, let him or his followers stand up in his place, and on his responsibility as a member, make that charge, and it will be investigated thoroughly and completely.
Again I said:
But there is something else to be said, and I repeat that, if my right hon. friend, or any of his followers, has any charge to make against a member of the Government in regard to any of these matters, let him make that charge in distinct and understandable terms, and he will have the investigation so soon as he so desires.
Again I said:
So far as our own affairs are concerned, so far as the actions of the members of the Government are concerned, these stand upon a different basis, and as to these I shall be prompt to accept any challenge that my right hon. friend or any of his followers may see fit to make in this House.
If a member of this House desires to make a charge against any member of the Government, or any member of the House, the proper coursq is for him to rise in his place, make a personal statement on his responsibility as a member of the House, and conclude the statement with a charge.
This has not been done, and thus the course which I am' about to announce is, strictly speaking, not demanded by any action which hon. gentlemen opposite have taken.. No one of them has risen'in his place and taken the responsibility of making a charge in the sense above set forth.
The hon. member for Richmond, N.S. (Mr. Kyte), however, made statements late on Tuesday evening as to the connection of the Minister of Militia, with certain contracts entered into by the Shell Committee, and as to enormous profits or commissions arising out of these contracts to certain companies which he mentioned. It is alleged that Mr. J. Wesley Allison had a very large interest in those profits or commissions, and it is suggested that through his influence with the Minister of Militia the Shell Committee were induced to make the contracts in question. The Minister of Militia and Defence had previously stated to the House his close relationship to Mr. J. Wesley Allison, and his great confidence in that gentleman.
Having regard to these considerations, I think it desirable that an inquiry should be made into the fuse contracts made by the Shell Committee with the American Ammunition Company and the International Arms and Fuse Company, and the cartridge-case contract made by the Shell Committee with the Edwards Valve Company.
Upon careful inquiry I cannot find that any of the other contracts, out of which it is alleged by the hon. member for Richmond that J. Wesley Allison obtained profits or commissions, were made either by the Shell Committee or by any department of the Government of Canada. However, as it has been alleged that the Shell Committee made a contract with the Providence Chemical Company of St. Louis, that alleged contract will be included.
I therefore propose to recommend to His

Royal Highness the Governor General that a. Royal Commission shall issue appointing one or more judges to make a thorough investigation into these four contracts and all matters connected therewith.
Since preparing the above statement, I have communicated with the two gentlemen whom I desired to appoint to the commission, and I have received their consent to act. They are Sir William Meredith, Chief Justice of the province of Ontario, and Mr. Justice Duff of the Supreme Court of Canada.
Two counsel will be appointed by the Government to act with the commission and to assist them. One of those counsel will be named by the Government; the other will he named by the right hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition. .
Yesterday I addressed the following cablegram to the Minister of Militia and Defence :
Ottawa, March 29, 1916.
Hughes, London.
. Following is synopsis of Kyte's statement in Shell Committee debate last evening. (Begins) :
On May twenty-fifth American Ammunition Company was incorporated. Minimum capital one thousand dollars and maximum one million.
' On June nineteenth last a contract was made between the Shell Committee and this company for the purchase of two million five hundred thousand fuses. It was signed by E. B. Cad-well as president of company, by General Bertram for Shell Committee and ratified and confirmed by General Hughes quote in accordance *with authority duly conferred upon me by His Britannic Majesty's Government unquote. There was to be an advance of dollars one million forty-one thousand six hundred on execution of agreement and dollars five hundred and twenty-three thousand eight hundred during first four months to assist company in financing contract. On June tenth, nineteen fifteen, ten days previously, an agreement had been made between B. F. Yoakum, E. W. Bassick and Cadwell reciting that Shell Committee had agreed to purchase two million five hundred thousand fuses from a manufacturer to be designated by E. B. Cadwell and Company, that Yoakum, Bassick and Cadwell and Company were together instrumental in negotiating and effecting said contract that Cadwell and Company Yoakum and Bassick were together entitled to receive as their commission for negotiating and effecting said contract the sum of one million dollars in the whole being at the rate of forty cents per fuse. The agreement went, on to divide this amount four hundred and seventy-five thousand to Yoakum two hundred and seventy-five thou-sant to Bassick and two hundred and fifty thousand to Cadwell and Company. The total was to be received by Cadwell and Company in first instance in trust for ail. Yoakum and Bassick agree to continue to use their"best endeavours to bring about the execution and delivery by said Shell Committee of said contract for two million five hundred thousanld fuses. Following or annexed to this an agreement signed by the American Ammunition Company by E. B. Cadwell, president to cause

to be paid to Cadwell and Company forty cents per fuse in accordance with the foregoing agreement if the contract for two million five hundred thousand fuses in such agreement mentioned is granted to us in acceptable form by Canadian authorities. At some date prior to January nineteen fifteen J. Wesley Allison and Eugene Lignanti had entered into an agreement to use their best endeavours for their mutual profit to procure as brokers contracts for supplies of exports to certain European countries. Later Benjamin F. Yoakum became associated with them. In September nineteen fifteen apparently because it was decided that Lignanti should withdraw, an agreement was made fixing the terms upon which certain commissions and profits* should be divided among them. This agreement recites that Yoakum procured contract of June nineteenth for American Ammunition Company from Shell (Committee and declares Lignanti entitled to fifty thousand dollars out of payments by company to Yoakum. Kyte asserts Allison and Yoakum were to share together in amounts remaining after Lignanti was paid. Then he alleges another contract procured by Yoakum from Shell Committee for Edward Valve Company to furnish five hundred thousand cartridge cases and that twenty thousand dollars commission less two thousand five hundred paid to Lignanti was to be divided between Yoakum and Allison. . Kyte also alluded to many other transactions in which Yoakum and Allison were to receive and divide commission of very large amounts but on inquiry none of them are found to relate to Shell Committee. (End synopsis.) I propose issuing Royal Commission forthwith to investigate fuse and cartridge case contracts and it is necessary that you return immediately for purpose of inquiry.
Borden.
To this I have received the following reply:
London, March 30, 1916.
Prime Minister,
Ottawa.
Please state to House on my behalf that I nave no improper connection with contracts referred to, or any other contracts. If any suggestion to the contrary is made I respectfully demand full investigation by the judicial tribunal presided over by Sir Charles Davidson. I shall sail first available boat.
Sam Hughes.
I also addressed yesterday a cable to Sir George Per ley giving a synopsis of Mt. Kyte's statements in the House in the same words as the synopsis cabled to General Sir Sam Hughes, and concluding as follows :
\
The minister's relation to Allison as described by himself in Parliament is so close that, although the expenditure is by the British Government and although such inquiries are unusual during progress of war, I feel it my duty to have Royal Commission issued forthwith to inquire into matters relating to Shell Committee above outlined, namely, fuse contract with American Ammunition Company and cartridge case contract with Edwards Valve Company. Please inform Colonial Secretary.
Borden.

I omitted to mention in that despatch one of the contracts to which I have alluded, so I despatched to Sir George Perley this morning a further message:
Ottawa, March 30, 1916.
Perley, Dominion.
London.
Referring to my message of yesterday the commission will include inquiry into contracts made by the Shell Committee with the International Arms and Fuse Company and a contract of which we can find no trace alleged to have been made by the shell Committee with the Providence Chemical Company of St. Louis for picric acid. Please inform Colonial Secretary.
Borden.
To neither of these messages to Sir George Perley have I yet received any reply.

Mr. Speaker, I regret to have to say to my right hon. friend and to the House that the proposal which he makes is absolutely unacceptable. If there is to be an inquiry, as he admits there ought to be an inquiry, that inquiry is to be made in this high court of Parliament. When Parliament is sitting no other court is acceptable. Therefore I ask for the resumption of the discussion upon my motion.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We will appoint a day to resume the discussion. I was not at all sure that any efforts the Government might make would satisfy my right hon. friend; but I am more concerned with the question as to whether this proposal will satisfy the people oif this country. I am absolutely convinced that it will satisfy them. I have announced the appointment of two judges whose names, I believe, will command confidence throughout the length and breadth of this country, and I have given to my right hon. friend the right to name one of the counsel to assist that commission. If that does not satisfy him I am -sure that any efforts on my part would be absolutely incapable of affording satisfaction to him.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
There is a way, and that is to grant a committee. That is all I ask; nothing less and nothing more. I again ask to have the discussion on my motion resumed.
-Sir ROBERT BORDEN: I will inform my right hon. friend -later as to that.

speechtext:
Motion agreed to, and the House proceeded to the consideration of the proposed resolution of Mr. Stevens as amended by the following amendment of Mr. R. B. Bennett:
That this House recognizes the great advance made during the past twenty years in the several provinces of Canada through the enactments of laws for promoting temperance and for prohibiting or restricting the liquor traffic.
That the restriction and regulation of the liquor traffic cannot be efficiently accomplished except through public opinion fully supporting enactments passed for that purpose.
That as public opinion varies in the several provinces it is desirable that such enactments depending for their efficient enforcement upon public opinion Should in the first instance be determined by the respective legislatures of the several provinces.
That up to the full measure of provincial jurisdiction the subject should in the first instance he dealt with by the respective provincial legislatures.
That this Parliament should at the present session enact legislation to prohibit the transportation of intoxicating liquor into any province for any use or purpose which is or may he forbidden by the law of such province.

Mr. Speaker, in support of the motion of the hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Stevens), which I bad the honour to second, I have received from various parts of the province of Quebec important resolutions which I think it is only fair to the House that I should communicate to them, because in the present circumstances very much importance is attached by the hon, member for Calgary (Mr. Bennett) to the fact that the province of Quebec has not officially accepted prohibition. That

was given by him as one of the reasons why the Bill of the Minister of Justice should be introduced, claiming that the proper course to follow was to leave the question of dealing with the liquor traffic to the various provinces, rather than to have legislation by the Dominion Parliament. When the Alliance representatives and others interested in prohibition met in Ottawa at the time of the last gathering here, it was proposed to ask in .the motion of the hon. member for Vancouver that this prohibition be for the period of the war and for three years afterwards, during the reconstruction period. That was eliminated from the resolution of the hon. member for Vancouver on the advice of certain people who thought it was more advisable to leave that part of the question to be dealt with by the Government, as circumstances might alter .cases. In the province of Quebec, the Anti-Alcoholic League had taken the position that for that province prohibition during the war period and for three years after the war would be unacceptable, and the Anti-Alcoholic League of Montreal, both English and French sections, transmitted to a large number of municipalities in the province the text of a resolution so drafted, asking the authorities to have it adopted. I want to communicate to the House a list of the municipalities which have adopted it, so as to dispel any impression which may exist here that, because the Legislature of Quebec has not adopted prohibition for the province, the feeling in that province is opposed to prohibition. When 916 municipalities out of 1,120 have of their own free will adopted prohibition and banished licenses from their limits; when in the whole district of Quebec, outside of the city of Quebec, there is not a single license; and when, if the liquor law of the province of Quebec could have been amended so as to enable a poll to be opened in every polling district in the city, the saloon would be banished from the city of Quebec; the House will understand that the feeling in favour of prohibition during the war, and for three years after the war, is very strong. The law of	Quebec is so	framed now that when a local option contest takes place we have only one poll in each municipality; therefore it is impossible to ask for a vote in the city of Montreal or the city of Quebec. That is what happened at St. Hyacinthe, a town of
12,000	or 13,000, where it took four days, I think, for the vote to be completed, and the provincial police had to be called in to

maintain order on the first day of the vote, the crowd at the -poll was so great. In the city of Three Rivers, the second largest city which adopted prohibition, and by an overwhelming majority, there Was also only one polling booth. lit is remarkable that during the last two years in every locality in the province of Quebec where a vote took place prohibition was carried by an overwhelming majority, with the single exception of St. Hyacinthe, where the women ha<^ no vote, and the town of Longueuil, which went weit by a small majority. In every other municipality in the province of Quebec where a vote was taken during the last two years prohibition was carried by an overwhelming majority. In the county of Pontiac the majority was over 1,000. That is a constituency of mingled French and English people. In Argenteuil the majority was up in the hundreds-, the tow'n of Lachute giving only four wet votes out of 300. And so it was all through the districts of Montreal and Quebec and the Eastern Townships and the district of Three Rivers. The impression prevails that the city of Montreal and the island of Montreal are strongly opposed to prohibition. That is a great mistake. I presented here the other day the petition of the town of St. Laurent, in Jacques Cartier, on the island of Montreal, signed by several hundred people, asking for prohibition during war time, and, in the list of resolutions and petitions which I shall have the honour to read a large number of parishes in the city and the various municipalities of Montreal are included. The feeling in favour of prohibition is very strong indeed. If a vote w'ere taken in Montreal to-morrow it is doubtful how it would go, but to imagine that prohibition would be rejected is a great mistake. The vote can not be taken in the city of Montreal under the provincial law, because we would have .only one polling booth. With the 130,000 voters in that city, polling would be practically impossible. But I know that a promise has been made on behalf of the local, Government that at the next session the law will be amended so as to have a polling booth for every polling district, and the vote will then be taken in Montreal. Bo I have no doubt that when this Parliament meets again at least eight, if not nine, provinces of the Dominion will have gone in for prohibition. Only one or two now remain non-prohibition, and-, in the province of Quebec a vote will be taken before another twelve months elapse, and then the Domin-148
ion Government will be in this position. So that, unless the Government create a federal district in Ottawa, the Dominion will be in this position, that eight out of nine provinces will have banished liquor so far as lies within their power. The people, during this war time, have taken a different view of this liquor question from that which they held before. People who were opposed to prohibition two years -ago, now favour it, because of the peculiar conditions through which the country is passing. The province of Ontario has afforded -an example in -that respect. Both political parties have joined hands, -and prohibition is now being brought in without a referendum. The liquor people realize full well that if a vote were taken, a prohibition measure would be carried by an overwhelming majority, if for no other than war reasons.
I do not wish to insist any longer upon the merits of prohibition, but I desire to say that the sentiment of Quebec is not opposed to prohibition to the etxtent which was sought to be shown 'in this House. An unfortunate statement was made- by one of my colleagues from the province of Quebec when he said that the clergy of the province had exercised an undue influence over the voters of that province, as regards prohibition. I have read a report of a Dominion Alliance meeting held in Toronto last night at which Mr. J. A. Roberts, secretary of the Dominion Alliance in the province of Quebec, -was one of the speakers. He explained the -attitude of the Roman Catholic clergy of the province of Quebec, gave them full credit for the great work they had done during recent years in favour of temperance, and contradicted the statement that any undue influence had been exercised. The olergy of the province of Quebec have taken up the cause of temperance, and have sought, toy every legitimate means, to impress upon the people the -awful curse, that liquor had been to many people throughout the oountry, and the necessity for those who are free from its evils to make a sacrifice for the good" of others during the exceptional period through which we are passing. I have other petitions which have come from all parts of the province of Quebec showing that all classes and nationalities in that province are in favour of prohibition during the war period and for three years thereafter for the purpose of reconstruction. I wish to read one communication from my own constituency showing that in that remote portion of the province of Quebec the feeling there is also favourable to prohibition. This letter reads:
Quebec Provincial Woman's Christian Temperance Union.
New Richmond, Que., March 20, 1916. The Hon. Charles Mareil, M.P.,
Ottawa.
Honourable Sir,-Please accept the sincere thanks of the members of the New Richmond Woman's Christian Temperance Union for your work in behalf of federal prohibition.
Not only the members of our Union, but all friends of temperance work in Canada, have been cheered and encouraged by your noble speech in the House of Commons.

I have a communication from the Presbytery of Toronto, which, having been published already, it is not necessary for me to read it. I have also a communication from the Ministerial Association of Montreal, showing that the English-speaking people generally in that city are strongly in favour of this measure. I have also received a resolution adopted by the Conservative Association of Westmount, a place from which liquor has been entirely banished. West-mount is looked upon as the most progressive part of the city of Montreal, and it is the part inhabited by the English-speaking people. We are proud of Westmount, from which liquor has been entirely banished. The Westmount Conservative Association has ad,opted a unanimous resolution asking for prohibition during war time and the reconstructive period after.
However, I suppose, now that the decision has been taken, it is useless for me to speak at any further length on this question, but I was anxious, in justice to the people of the province of Quebec, to show that they are strongly in favour of prohibition, that aheady 900 municipalities have gone in for it, that they have asked for nothing better than to have it adopted, that in the whole district of Quebec, outside of the city itself, they have adopted it, that the city of Quebec will adopt it as soon as polling facilities can be arranged to have a vote taken, and that the same thing will happen in Montreal.
I did not want a slur to be cast upon the province of Quebec by having the impression go abroad that when the 4 p.m. English-speaking provinces of the Dominion were going in for prohibition, not only for economic, but for moral reasons, the province of Quebec was standing aside, or was lukewarm in the matter. Far from that being the case, I am convinced, that if the opportunity were furnished to people of the province of Quebec they would adopt prohibition by an overwhelming majority, not only in the districts of Quebec and of Three Rivers, and in the Eastern Townships, where it has already carried, but even in the district of Montreal itself. I think that will come later on. I shall not discuss the merits of this Bill introduced by my horn, friend the Minister of Justice; I shall reserve any remarks I have to make on that subject until later.

I wish to say a word. Had I known that the resolution moved by 
my hon. friend from Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) was to be voted upon the other evening I would have been here, an<} would have voted for his resolution and against the amendment. However, as the amendment has carried, I do not feel that I would be justified in' voting against the resolution as amended. While not going as far as the resolution of the hon. member for Vancouver, it certainly is a step in the right direction, and will enable the provinces thoroughly to carry out any law they may see fit to enact on the subject.

I was not present in the House on Monday last, when the motion was before the House, but if I had been present I would have voted for the motion of the hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Stevens), and against the amendment of the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Bennett). As the amendment of the hon. member for Calgary was adopted, I am now prepared to support it, as there is nothing else upon the Order Paper, but I would have preferred to have supported the motion as it originally stood.

I have only one word to say in connection with the vote which will be taken, and that is that I will vote, if I am in the House-although I must leave in a few minutes-for the resolution as amended. I voted against the amendment because I thought the amendment did not go far enough. I was in favour of the resolution of the hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Stevens), seconded by the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil). As the majority of the House saw fit to amend the resolution and to place in its stead the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Bennett) and leave only upon the Order Paper this half measure, and as I consider that a half measure of temperance is better than no measure at all, the same as a half loaf of bread is better than no bread at all, I must, not with pleasure but because I am unable to do anything else, support the motion as amended.

I hoped to have had an opportunity to vote for the motion of the hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Stevens), and 1 did vote, when this question was up the other day, against the amendment, because I stood in the same position as my bon, friend from Shefford (Mr. Boivin). The amendment, to my mind, did not go far enough. This question of the

prohibition of the liquor traffic is a question that belongs to us in this House. We cannot throw the responsibility on the legislatures, which, as we all know, do not possess the power to prohibit the manufacture and importation of intoxicating liquors. It is true that a number of provinces have attempted to prohibit the sale, but constitutionally they have not the power. The amendment, and the Bill of the Minister of Justice-I presume the Bill will follow the amendment-do not even profess to prohibit the manu.'aciure of intoxicating liquors in provinces where prohibition l.ae been adopted, and they are defective to that extent. If the amendment went so far as to prohibit the manufacture of intoxicating liquors in every province where public sentiment was in favour of it, and had voted for it, there would be an additional reason for supporting the amendment; but I understand that it does not go that far. There is no doubt to my mind that public opinion' in this country is strongly in favour of absolute prohibition. I have always hesitated somewhat on this question, fearing that public opinion was not behind it sufficiently to justify my voting for absolute prohibition, 'but I feel satisfied that a great change has taken place in public sentiment on this question during the last year or two. For proof of that, we have only to observe what is happening in the various provinces. As we have already been reminded, Prince Edward Island has adopted prohibition; Nova Scotia joined the ranks a few days ago; Ontario, the premier province, is falling into line; Manitoba has already adopted it; Saskatchewan too, to a 'limited extent, and I understand that prohibition was brought in force in Alberta by a popular vote of some 26,000. So that six of the nine provinces composing the Confederation have already declared in favour of prohibition, which shows conclusively that public sentiment at the present time is overwhelmingly in favour of absolute prohibition. If the Government was amenable to the [DOT] view of the people of Canada, they would adopt the resolution, but it appears they are not willing to go that far. For my part, I propose to support any temperance measure brought down, on the principle, as the hon. member for Shef-ford has said, that half a measure is better than none at all. I fear, however, that what is proposed is not even half a measure. I have not yet had the opportunity to sift it thoroughly, but from what I have seen of it
it seems to me to be a gold brick, and of very little use. It does not even prohibit the sale by merchants in an outside province. It provides that a merchant must not send liquor into a dry province, but no penalty is provided for selling it. That, to my mind, is the real question. A merchant who exports into a dry province should be liable to prosecution. It would be very easy for a merchant to evade this Bill by simply handing over the work of transporting the liquor to somebody else; the truckman who carries the liquor away from the shop will be the one to pursue if the Bill remains in its present form. I think the Bill is very little good,,but in the hope that it may be improved in committee, and satisfy to some extent the public sentiment of the country, I shall support it. I very much regret that I have not the opportunity to support a measure that would bring about absolute prohibition of the liquor traffic in Canada.

I also
wish to join with previous speakers in saying that I should have been glad to support the resolution submitted by the hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Stevens), if I had been present on Monday. But as that resolution is off the Order Paper at the present time, I shall gladly support the Government measure, as it is the only one now before us that seeks to advance the cause of temperance.

I had thought that I should have had an opportunity for expressing my views on prohibition by voting on the resolution introduced by the hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Stevens), and not being fully acquainted with Parliamentary procedure, I was surprised that we were not given that opportunity. I want now to place myself on record as being in sympathy with a measure for absolute prohibition, and if it is impossible to record my vote in that way, then I am in favour of the prohibition measure brought down l)y the Government. I believe that measure, if properly enforced, and with co-operation between the federal Government and the provinces, wdl be of some assistance, probably of great assistance in maintaining the cause of prohibition in the different provinces.
Mr. J. A. MicMILLAN (Glengarry): Like the other members on this side of the House, I was rather at sea the other night as to what stand I should take. I was certainly in favour of the resolution


of the hon. member for Vancouver, but being denied the privilege of supporting it, I did the next best thing .and voted against the amendment. I have very good reasons for feeling that the resolution introduced toy the toon, member for Vancouver should 'be supported and become law, for I am situated very much like the people of Ottawa will be if Ontario goes dry. They are close to Hull, which I am afraid will be Hell, when Ontario goes dry. I voted for the amendment of the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Bennett) the other night, as I thought it brought the matter before the House in a more tangible form .for the present than the resolution of the hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Stevens), and furthermore, because the Bill already 'brought down by the Government embodied the provisions of that resolution. The seconder of the resolution says that public opinion in the province of Ontario is largely in favour of prohibition. I do not doubt that that is the case, and it is very probable that the Legislature of Quebec will soon enact a measure of prohibition for that province -a measure which will be more welcome to them than if it were imposed upon them by this Parliament. My hon. friend from Guystoorough (Mr. Sinclair) says that prohibition should be dealt with by this Parliament. It is true that this Parliament, under the constitution, has jurisdiction in matters of trade and commerce, and therefore jurisidiction over the liquor traffic, if that may be said to come under the heading of trade and commerce. But it is also a matter of local concern; it affects the habits of the people. This country is very large in territory, including nine provinces, and the habits of the people may vary very considerably; and a law of this kind must have strong public opinion 'behind it, if it is to be properly enforced. When we have the verdict of the people of the different provinces in favour of prohi-

bition, it will be easier for this Parliament to pass a measure for Dominion-wide prohibition and to ensure its enforcement. I consider the amendment proposed by my hon. friend from Calgary (Mr. R. B. Bennett), which will be carried out by the Bill before the House, a great step towards temperance and prohibition, and I prefer to support it to supporting the main resolution, because I think we should obtain the opinion of the different provinces before enacting Dominion-wide prohibition. In that way it will be more certain that we will have prohibition this year.

Mr. Speaker, I am sorry I cannot at this moment support the opinion expressed by my hon. friend from Prescott (Mr. Proulx). I would have been only too glad to vote in favour of the resolution moved by the hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Stevens), and seconded by the hon. member for Bonaven-ture (Mr. Marcil), because I believe it would meet the current of public opinion which is daily growing stronger in favour of total prohibition throughout the Dominion. That opinion was not so strong in times past for the reason, I believe, that, prohibition being confined to the provinces, it was felt that the provinces could not enact laws that would prohibit in a manner satisfactory to the people; but at the present time, confronted as we are with this terrible war, the people of Canada have come to realise that the time has come for them to ask the Federal Parliament to enact a law that will prohibit the manufacture and sale of intoxicating liquors throughout the Dominion.
In New Brunswick, besides the Scott Act, we have also the Temperance Parish Act, with which my hon. friends from New Brunswick are well acquainted, and which has worked better than the Scott Act just because it is confined to a smaller number of people who take a direct interest in the matter. At present, however, there is a complaint that liquor is introduced once in a while into the different parishes. In the county of Gloucester, which I have the honour to represent, the Temperance Parish Act is in force in every parish with the exception of the shire town of Bathurst. If that shire town has not taken that step towards local prohibition, it is just because there was an opinion that the time was coming when prohibition would be introduced by the local Government or by the Federal Government. There is to-day, before the legislature of New Brunswick, a

proposition to enact a provincial temperance measure. In the meantime, we in New Brunswick feel that neither provincial nor parochial action will ever be effective. We should take heed to the trend of public opinion and I believe in this time of war, from economic as well as moral Conditions, the people and the Parliament of this country should seriously consider if the resolution moved by the hon. member for Vancouver is the one that should be adopted by this Government. I have as much consideration as any other hon. member for the principle of personal liberty which I have always honoured and respected; but human life calls for personal sacrifice, mutual sacrifice, sacrifice for the weak and the poor and the needy, and under the present conditions the trend of public opinion is that the Federal Parliament rather than the provincial legislatures should enact a prohibitory measure.
In the province of Quebec, if there has not been such an Act as there is in the other provinces, it is rather because the people there feel that a provincial Act would [DOT] not be sufficient to enforce prohibition. Therefore, if I am given the opportunity, I shall be pleased to vote for the resolution moved by the hon. member for Vancouver. In the meantime, I will certainly support any measure in favour of prohibition, because, as was said by the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Boivin) half a loaf is better than no bread at all, but only for that reason.

Mr. Speaker, if the resolution as amended by the amendment of the hon. member for Calgary means an expression of opinion in favour of temperance, then I wish to put myself on record as being in favour of temperance. That the province of Ontario will in any way suffer, as my hon. friend (Mr. McMillan) said a few moments ago, by being too near Hull, I want to say at once, being the representative of the county in which the city of Hull happens to find itself, that the province of Ontario through its close proximity to the city of Hull will learn many lessons of liberty and morality. I am not going to speak of the effect of the proposed resolution upon any portion of the province of Quebec; I merely arose to say that I would be in favour of the resolution pm posed by the hon. member for Vancouver, but, as it has been amended, through a very clever ruse, I should judge, I am sorry to 'have to vote for the amendment.
I would very much have preferred to vote for the resolution of the hon. member for Vancouver, but I will vote for the amendment as being the only way in which I can express my opinion in favour of temperance.

Mr. Speaker, in regard to this resolution which is now before the House, we have a peculiar situation, due to the result of the operation of the rules of debate. Hon. gentlemen who are in favour of this Parliament enacting Dominion-wide legislation, prohibiting the manufacture anc( sale of intoxicating liquor, as alone this Parliament can do, have before them a resolution which is offered in substitution of the original resolution, and in which there is a certain conclusion arrived at, it seems to me, wholly inconsistent with the original resolution. For instance, paragraph 4 of the resolution as amended by the hon. member for Calgary, asks this House to come to the conclusion:
That up to the full measure of provincial jurisdiction the subject should in the first instance be dealt with by the respective provincial legislatures.
One could hardly conceive any Parliamentary 'declaration so absolutely opposed to the proposition declared in the resolution moved by the hon. member for Vancouver. Prima facie he represented the temperance people of this country, asking this Parliament to deal with the liquor traffic as only Dominion legislation effectively can deal with it by stopping its manufacture and importation. The declaration of my hon. friend from Calgary is that that is not the right thing to do at all; he says that you must wait until a provincial law is passed before moving one step. That seems to me, from the standpoint of those who are interested, in the cause of temperance, to be a retrograde step. If this Parliament passes the resolution as amended every member who votes for it will give expression to the proposition that it is of no use for the temperance people coming to this Parliament and asking it to take a step towards prohibiting the manufacture and importation of intoxicating liquors, but that they must first go to the provincial legislatures and ask them to pass prohibitory laws.
Let me give an illustration of the effect of this resolution and the proposed legislation oif the Minister of Justice. A well-known lawyer in my province has called my at-

tention to the situation in Nova Scotia. The declaration in that resolution and in the Bill is to the effect that Parliament should
-enact legislation to prohibit the transportation or importation of intoxicating liquor into any province for any use or purpose which is or may be forbidden by the law of such province.
Unless you have a provincial enactment covering the bounds of each specific province, this legislation of the Minister of Justice, I submit, will be absolutely null and inoperative. In our province there is what is known as the Nova Scotia License Act operative in sixteen counties. In the county of Guysborough we have a federal act in operation, the Canada Temperance Act. Ini Annapolis also we have the Canada Temperance Act in effect', though a vote has [DOT]been taken for the purpose of defeating it and the question of the legality of the election is still sub judice. The result is, that, if the legislation proposed by the hon. meimber for Calgary and the Minister of Justice goes into effect, it will be quite legal to import into Nova Scotia any liquor that one may wish to bring in, because there is no 'provincial law covering the whole province. A person in the county of Guysborough would have the right under the Canada Temperance Act to import-

gentleman aware that in 1908 the Canada Temperance Act was amended to meet the very case he suggests? That amendment would prohibit the importation into Guysborough county, which has adopted the Scott Act, of liquor from non Scott Act area, for the purpose of violating the Scott Act in that province.

The hon. gentleman forgets that there ie nothing in the Scott Act to prevent the importation of liquor for personal use. The people of Guysborough can import for personal use all the liquor they want, and under the proposed legislation of the Minister of Justice and of the hon. member for Calgary it will not be possible to prevent it. AH that need toe done is to have the liquor that is brought across the line from New Brunswick, or brought into a seaport of Nova Scotia, directed to the county of Guysborough, and this law will be inoperative so far as it is concerned. And if the Supreme Court of Nova Scotia declares that in Annapolis county the Canada TemperfMr. Macdonald.1
ance Act is in force, you will have the same condition there. So, yon have a splendid illustration of the absurdity of the legislation proposed-of the juggling with this question carried on by the Government. I am surprised that my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster), whose long 'advocacy of temperance legislation has won the admiration of those interested in the cause, should not 'have pressed for a practical dealing with this *problem by measures which would at least restrict the manufacture and importation of liquor .if not blot it out altogether. Hon. gentlemen who have anything to do with the enforcing of law know that it is utterly absurd to think of enforcing .prohibitory legislation if Parliament ensures the continuance of the legality of the manufacture and importation of liquor. If you permit the manufacture, what is the use of saying that the liquor shall not toe sold here, or shall not be 6old there? The sale will go on in spite of such legislation. The result that I have indicated .in my own province, I am sure, would work out in other parts of the Dominion also. Therefore, I regret this -resolution offered by my hon. friend from 'Calgary (Mr. K. B. Bennett). Many hon. gentlemen in this House who are sincerely in favour of prohibitory legislation, I am sure, will regard it as absolutely inoperative and of no value whatever.

I endorse what the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) has said. The resolution introduced by the hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) was prohibitory legislation, but this other legislation is to a great exent a farce. So far as Ontario is concerned, it will allow as much liquor to come into the province as ever. It will confine the sale to druggists, wholesale and retail. Anybody who has had experience oi the Scott Act, as I have had, knows how much better the change from hotels to druggists will be. I do not know what they will have under this legislation, but then they had blank certificates that they filled up. W'hat good is the temperance legislation that permits that kind of thing? I do not pretend to be a temperance man by any manner of means; tout I do pretend not to be a hypocrite. The resolution of the hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) goes to the kernel of the question, for it prohibits the .manufacture and importation of spirituous liquors. Why don't we vote that straight and put it into effect, if we

want temperance legislation? If we don't want it, why don't we say so? What is the use of shuffling it from one class to another if the sale is to be allowed? As to this resolution I confess that, while it might be a catch for those in favour of the resolution of the hon. member for Vancouver, I believe the temiperaneepeople will understand it just as well as we understand it, and the catch will not be of great benefit to the Government that brings it into effect.

I would infer from the remarks of the hon. member that he is in favour of passing legislation which will prohibit any private individual having in his possession, or purchasing, any liquor in any quantity whatever.

Quite right. I am absolutely in favour of total prohibition, or of letting the people buy it as they want it, one or the other. I may add, I have never found the necessity for liquor so far as I am personally concerned, and I doubt that it is a benefit to anybody else. -

speakeroldname: Hon. J. D. HAZEN (Minister of Marine and Fisheries):
speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: This is the amount that was asked for last year. The amount we spent in 1914-15 was $275,950.71. The expenditure for the current year, up to the 31st December, was $187,103.40. Out of this vote are paid salaries and disbursement of the different fisheries officers and guardians, and the expenses also of the Advisory Board.
How much does the minister expect will be expended during the current year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: This vote is largely for salaries, and there is not much difference in the expenditure from year to year. I should think we would expect to spend the same amount as we did last year. For the current year I would estimate the expenditure to be about $275,000.

Does not the minister think he should reduce the vote by $30,000? It may not be a very large reduction, but still it would be setting an example that might well he followed in all of the departments. In the aggregate the amount would be considerable. In the year
5 p.m. before last this total was not expended by $30,000, and the result has been the same for the current year. Should not the minister make a reduction?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The appropriations this
year for fisheries are reduced by over $200,000. We have made up these Estimates with due regard for economy, and my officers thought it would not be altogether safe to have a less amount than that which is provided for in the vote. We may not expend the full amount; we will spend as little as we can, having regard to the public interest. I think it would be better to leave it as it is. I do not think anything will be gained by reducing the amount, because we will not spend the full amount unless we have to.

The gain of it is this: the Minister of Finance necessarily must have regard to the Estimates that are placed before him by the different ministers. He is proposing now to impose very heavy taxes upon the people of the country. The Minister of Finance must have not only money enough to provide for the interest on the war loan, but to carry on the ordinary and necessary services of the country. If this committee passes large amounts, amounts in excess of what will be required, it is not acting fairly either towards the country or the gentleman who is charged with the financing of the country. It does seem to me that the minister ought not to ask this committee for anything more than he thinks will 'be absolutely necessary. The minister says that he is not asking for as much as was voted last year. One of the items in which a reduction might be made is that for a fish-

eries exhibit at the -Canadian National Exhibition.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We have reduced, that.
It is reduced by a small amount, but I think that in war time that might well be reduced.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Our experience last year shows us how we can do it more cheaply.
I suggest to my hon. friend a reduction of at least $30,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I would not have any hesitation at all in acceding to my hon. friend's request and reducing this amount by $15,000 but fox the reason that there is the outstanding matter in regard to the fisheries which the hon. member for Bonaven-ture (Mr. Marcil)has several times referred to; that is the question of the jurisdiction over tidal fisheries in the province of Quebec. The question is as to who shall administer these fisheries. The matter is under process of negotiation between the Department of Justice, it being a legal question, and the Department of the Attorney General of Quebec. If, before the expiration of the year for which these Estimates are being voted, a decision should be given by the court to the effect that the administration of these fisheries in the tidal waters comes under -the control of the Federal Government, as we believe it does, we would have to make a certain expenditure of money amounting to about $15,000. We will not expend any of this money unless the decision is given, but we would be placed in rather an awkward position if a decision were given during the year, and if, in order to administer these fisheries, we had, to ask for a Governor General's warrant.
Has the question been submitted to the oourts, or is it still under negotiation?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The questions which are to be submitted to the courts have been agreed upon between the Department of Justice and tlhe Attorney General of Quebec. They will very' soon go before the courts with the understanding that from the decision of the court in Quebec there will lie an appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada. '

Some hon. gentlemen on this side of tlhe House have been hoping that the minister

would make a general statement regarding the progress of the fishing industry in Canada during the past year, and outline what he intended to do for the future. That policy has been adopted by several departments of the Government, such as the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Railways and Ganals, and I regard it as a good policy, which I commend to the consideration of the minister. My hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley) has raised a question of economy. It perhaps is a waste of time to talk economy to the present administration. We do not seem to have made much progress in that direction at the present session. It has frequently been suggested from this side of the House that ministers should economize, but none of our suggestions have been accepted. Only last night we came across an item in the Estimates of the Secretary of State for $15,000 for the purchase of wooden whales, Buffalo skeletons, wasps' nests, Indian relics, and things of that kind. We considered that it was an item that should riot be voted at a time like this, when money was so scarce and we are engaged in such a costly war. We addressed ourselves to the Secretary of State and to the Minister of Public Works; we addressed him as a statesman, as a Christian, as a Canadian-
But not as an economist.

Yes, as an economist, also. We felt that this money should not be spent, but saved and applied towards carrying on the war. But it was of no use. After all our eloquence, the Minister of Public Works and the Secretary of State cracked the party whip, and the motion to cut out the item was voted down. The money is now at the disposal of the Government for the purchase of these wooden whales and Indian relics, but they must justify their action before the country.

I think the minister said
it was not likely the money would be spent this year.

Yes, but we were not
satisfied with that; we wanted to be absolutely certain the money would not be spent. I have looked over the Estimates of my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries in a general way, and wish to draw his attention to the fact that there has been an enormous increase in the expenditure on the Fisheries Branch since he took office. In the, four and a half years
that my hon. friend has had charge of the department the expenditure has practically doubled. Now, if we were getting results equivalent to the expenditure, we would not complain, tout I submit that we are not, and I do not think the expenditure can be justified. There is no expenditure that could 'be made in connection with the fisheries branch that I should not feel justified in supporting, if the expenditure were made in such a way as to build up our fisheries, and make it the great industry it ought to be. But the only thing that ihas grown up in connection with the fisheries is the expenditure. There has been practically no growth in the industry itself. In the year 1910-11, the last year for which hon. gentlemen on this side of the House were responsible, according to Public Accounts, page 868, the total expenditure on the fisheries branch was $760,734.69; in 1911-12 it has increased to $843,856.98; in 1912-13,	$921,953.14; in 1913-14,	$1,229,519.19; in
1914-15, $1,465,360.65. The increase in the annual expenditure on the fisheries branch since my hon. friend took charge of the department has been the enormous sum of $704,625.96, or 'almost double the expenditure when the present Administration took office. The estimate for this year is $1,224,900, which, it is true, is some $200,000 less than, last year's estimate, but I think it will be very difficult for my hon. friend to explain the enormous increase that 'has taken place in the fisheries branch since he took charge. There has been no corresponding increase in the trade. The output has not increased in proportion to the expenditure. In looking over the fisheries report which was submitted to the House a -few days ago, I find that the growth of the industry ha3 been very slow, especially in Eastern Canada. In 1885, thirty years ago, the total value of the fisheries in Nova Scotia was $8,283,922, and in 1915, the last year for which we have a report, the total output was valued at $7,730,191. In those thirty years there has apparently been no increase in the industry in Nova Scotia. On the contrary, the output has decreased by $500,000. In New Brunswick, in 1885, the value of the fisheries was $4,005,031, and in 1915, $4,940,083. That is a small increase. In Prince Edward Island, in 1885, the value of the output was $1,293,430, and in 1915, $1,261,666. In the Maritime Provinces as a whole, in 1885 the total value of the output was $13,583,783, and in 1915, $13,931,940. So

we have been marking time, so far as our fisheries are concerned for the last thirty years. The question might very properly be asked, and, indeed, ought to be asked, why has no progress been made in the fishing industry in Eastern Canada? I think the answer, will readily occur to my hon. friend, and to every hon. gentleman *who has studied this question. It is the long haul necessary to get our fish on the Canadian market, and the fact that we have never had a fair chance to develop the American market. The difficulty is that we are fighting against geography in our efforts to develop the fishing industry. Our Government is paying a large sum of money to have our fish transported to Montreal, Toronto, and other large centres. That is all right as far as it goes, but the industry cannot grow because the demand in those places is comparatively small. We have been told by some witnesses who were examined before the committee that a carload of fish is too much to send to the city of Toronto from the eastern coast, that the fish could not be sold, that a carload would be too much to force on the market at one time. You can send as many carloads of fish as you like to Boston because it is a great distributing centre and the fish go from Boston to New York, Chicago, St. Louis and all the other American cities, so that there is practically no limit to the fish that could be absorbed in that distributing centre.
What about Montreal?

Some fish comes from Boston to Montreal, but not a very great deal at the present time. There is a duty on fish imported from the United States and the Government assists in bringing fish from the eastern coast to Montreal. That has, I think, to a large extent, lessened the American trade with Canadian cities, but that has not helped us very much because we never can build up a big trade with the comparatively small population we have in Canada. Why do we not do something more to develop the American market? There is every reason in favour of such a course. There is the cheap water carriage along the eastern seaboard from Boston to New York, which ought to count a good deal of itself. The American market is our nearest market; we can reach it in about twenty-four hours by a fast steamboat, a shorter time than we can reach the city of Montreal in by rail. Hon. gentlemen must remember there is no product in the world that is so perishable

as fresh fish. I am told by experts that if it is exposed to the sun it begins to depreciate within ten minutes after it is taken out of the water, and consequently it is with great difficulty that it can be placed on a distant market, and it cannot be done at all unless you have the best facilities, which we do not have in Canada. You would hardly believe, Sir, that after thirty years of experience in this business, after thirty years of public ownership of a railway connecting the Maritime provinces with the province of Quebec, we are not to-day ir a position to send a box of fresh fish m a refrigerator car by express; it fias to be sent in a heated car and it cannot ordinary-ily arrive at its destination in good condii tiion. The dealers will tell you that by the time the fish arrives at Montreal, the heat of the car has melted the ice and the fish is soft and not suitable for the market. I may say, however, that we have a better chance in the case of freight, because for carload lots of fish, refrigerator cars are provided that -will take the fish, either frozen or not frozen, to Montreal in very good condition. But why should we not have express as well as freight facilities? Carriage by freight ds slow in any case: it takes over two days to reach Montreal from the Maritime provinces; very often it takes several days longer owing to trains being delayed in various ways. I understand that the service has been very bad during the last few months. No one, however, is complaining very much of the freight service, but there is good reason to complain of the express service on the Intercolonial railway at the present time.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman said
.that the express service was bad. Did he mean the express or the freight service?

The express service. 1 have no special complaint to make of the freight except that it lis too slow.
Mr. HA25EN: I suppose my hon. friend refers to the facilities on the cars rather than to the time taken in delivering the goods.

By express, yes. I understand the facilities on the express cars are very poor at the present time, and I hope the Government will do something in the way of improving them.
IMr. HAZEN: I am not going to quarrel with you about that.

Mr. SINCLAIR I am not going to discuss that question because it will come out later on when the committee, dealing with that matter, reports to the House. A few weeks ago I asked this question:
Has the Government considered the question of transportation of fresh fish from the Atlantic coast of Nova Scotia to the American market?
The answer I received was:
Since the examination and discussion of this question that we had two years ago the government have given no apparent attention to it, although generally, it has been kept in mind.
It is difficult for me to understand how the Government can keep a thing in mind generally, and at the same time not think of it for two years. It is something like the story of Rip van Winkle, who, when he went to sleep, had stored away in the back of his mind recollections of his wife and family and home, and other things, and it might be expected when he awoke he would remember all about them. We have no guarantee that this Government will ever waken up on this question, and if we can do anything to waken them up we should do it, because the question of an entrance into the American market for the fish of the Maritime Provinces is one of great importance for the development of this industry.^ Why should we not assist in the transportation of fish to the United States? The individual fisherman cannot build steamers; they cannot run railways nor secure the services of refrigerator cars unless those facilities are provided for them in some way. It is the function of the Government to do that kind of work, and I can scarcely understand the position taken by this Government when they take the ground that they should not promote any business that goes in' the direction of the United States. It makes no difference to the fisherman, provided that he gets a profitable return for the fish he catches, where it goes. It is the same with our wheat. We cannot consume it all in Canada, and we can never develop our western wheat areas if we adopt that policy. I heard one of my hon. friends from the West state a few nights ago that only 10 per cent of the arable land in the province of Alberta was under cultivation, and only 18 per cent of the arable land in the province of Saskatchewan. When all that land is ploughed, where are we going to find our market? Why should we not find the nearest, and best market for these natural products, not only wheat, but fish? Take our lumber industry. Where would it be
if we tabooed the American market? Why, Sir, we have no other market at the present time. It costs too much at present to send our lumber across the Atlantic, and we might as well stop our saw mills and abandon our lumber industry if we do not endeavour to exploit the American market. The situation in regard to fish is this, that there is no way in eastern Nova Scotia for the merchants or fishermen to reach the American market with the present facilities, and I submit the Government should take some action. The case is different in western Nova Scotia. Great progress has been made in Yarmouth, our most western town, in that regard. Our lamented friend, Mr Law, the very day of his death, made a very interesting speech in the House of Commons, in which he pointed out that the business had grown enormously in the town of Yarmouth during the last two or three years. I have not the exact figures of what it was a few years ago; but he told us that in 1915- the export of fish and fish products from the port of Yarmouth to Boston amounted to $1,668,111, or one-quarter of the total output from the whole province of Nova Scotia. That has resulted from the fact that transportation facilities have been provided. Between Yarmouth and Boston there is a line of steamships in connection with the Canadian Pacific railway. In the summer season, when the tourist traffic is on, the service is daily, and during the rest of the year it is three times a week. Since that service has been provided and the Americans have opened their market by making fish free of duty, the fish trade has sprung up in Yarmouth, so that the large sum of money I have mentioned was received by the fishermen for their product during the last year. The same thing could happen in various places along the coast of Nova Scotia if equal facilities were given to reach the American market. That is the question I put up to my hon. friend the minister, and it is the biggest question in relation to this matter that he can tackle.
If the minister will look over the history of the department he will nnd that we have really made no progress in thirty years in expanding this business. Surely he must see that there is something wrong. We have the men on the coast to catch the fish, and we have a prolific fishery. , If we have made no advance in the output it is simply because we have not been able to reach the only market that is available to us, the market of the United States. The testimony of Mr. Ward Fisher might be worth reading to my hon. friend. Mr. Fisher, I

understand, did all lie could to prevent the reciprocity treaty from coming into force. He is a supporter of the present Administration and one of its officers. In the last report on fisheries I find the following testimony by Mr. Fisher:
The revised American tariff resulted in the establishment of a number of new companies. Three were established in Yarmouth county. The ready market approved and prices secured, greatly revived the fisheries of this county, and was the cause of a considerable number of men fishing from home instead of from United States ports. This latter effect was true, also, in other counties.
That is the testimony of a gentleman who opposed, the reciprocity treaty, hut who, after the markets of the United States were thrown open to our products, discovered that it was a splendid thing for the fisheries of Nova Scotia, and is honest enough to say so.
A step was taken by my hon. friend the Minister of Naval Affairs in connection with the Fisheries Department that he has never, so far as I know, explained to the House. A year or two ago he transferred the fisheries to the Department of the Naval Service. I quite understand that is a matter of administration, and the minister might say that it was an internal question that the department alone has to do with. But it is a matter of considerable importance, and I do not think it should have been done in a corner ana without a reason having been given to the House. What can officers of the navy know about fisheries: -that is, if they are really naval officers. If we are to have a navy it should, not be a sham navy, or maintained for show. Its officers should devote their whole time to naval affairs. They should study, for instance, the best method of winning battles and the latest build of war vessels. They ought to know every harbour on the coast, and not only ought they to know our own coast, but they ought to know the seven seas-the waters throughout the world; they ought to know them as intimately as my hon. friend (Mr. Hazen) knows the mud flats of Courtenay bay. Besides we might as well turn over agriculture to the Militia Department as to turn over fisheries to the Naval Department. And just think what would happen if, while the country was engaged in war, and the attention of the Minister of Militia and his chief deputy is required to be given closely to the attention of the defence of the country, they had to deal with such questions as the potato bug, or the coddling moth, or hog
pi]'. Sinclair.]
cholera, or some other such problem with which the Department of Agriculture has to deal. It may be said that the fishery officers in the Naval Department will look after fisheries. But the man who directs the work of the department is the deputy minister, and what would happen if, in time of war, he were involved in studying such questions as lobster regulations, the close seasons for clams, pickled fish, and all those other intricate questions that come before a fishery officer? That is what is bound to happen under the system that my hon. friend has adopted. Let me remind him of what happened in 1914 when the war broke out. We were not in any way prepared, for it. It is on record that the Njobe, the only warship we had in eastern Canada was practically out of commission. She was lying in the harbour of Halifax with barnacles on her; the sailors were deserting the ship, and some of the machinery was stored in a warehouse on a wharf. During that time the naval staff of Canada, apparently, was employed in editing a little book called " Fish and How to Cook it." For that book came out about the time of the declaration of war. I received my copy on the 6th of August, and war was declared, as we all know, on the 4th of August. At the time of the naval debate, the leader of the present Government, then leader of the Opposition, put a question to my honoured leader (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), then Prime Minister. That question was-something like this: Suppose that.a Canadian warship meets an enemy warship on the high seas, war not having been declared; will she fight? He got the answer he wanted, a proper answer. Sir Wilfrid said:	She will not fight until
ordered to do so by the Government that controls her. That is the answer he wanted, and it enabled him to misrepresent my right hon. leader to a certain element in this country.
If this system is going to be carried on, and the question is asked of this Government: Will the ships controlled by the present administration figlht? I think the answer would have to be: No, 'but that she can show the other fellow how to cook fish! That is really the only thing that the Naval Department has done so far, of which we know anything.
Do they even know how to do that?

consideration of both of these questions to my hon. friend. The fisheries of British Columbia have developed simply because they have been able to get into the American market by means of the enterprising methods adopted by the Canadian Pacific Railway and 'by the Dominion Express Company. The fisheries of British Columbia have made much greater progress than the fisheries of the Atlantic coast, yet the 'largest market they have is in the Eastern United States, and they are able to reach that market because the Canadian Pacific Railway has been enterprising enough to give them adequate transportation facilities. I trust that these suggestions may not be lost on my hon. friend.

I have already referred to the matter of transportation by express, and as that will come before this committee when the Fisheries Committee make their report to the House I shall not take up the time of this committee at the moment. I see by item 260 that the amount of money asked for is to include the expenses of the Fisheries Advisory Board. I have often wondered what great good we get from this Board. The minister, when making his statement, will perhaps tell us some of the good things it has done in the interest of Canada.' I also see by number 272 that the minister proposes another new venture, if I may so call it. He now proposes that the officers shall examine and inspect the canning factories for fish. There is already on the statute-books provision fox the inspection of our fruit factories, those that pack fruit and vegetables; but we have not had any inspection of fish canning factories. If this is intelligently carried out it is quite possible that good may come from it. But, as a matter of fact, I do not think there is really very much for the inspectors of pickled fish now in the employ of the department to do, and it is just possible that the minister has in view that these officers may also undertake the inspection of fish packing. I am sure' that if we had a report of the work of these men since their appointment we would have some queries as to what we had received in return for the money expended. I want to congratulate the minister in several respects. He has acted wisely "in continuing the transportation service which was inaugurated some years ago by paying a share of the express rates to the inland cities of Canada. I rather differ with my hon. friend (Mr. 
Sinclair) for this reason: I felt that that service when it was inaugurated was to encourage the consumption of Canadian fish in the Canadian centres. I believe that, generally, it has done that. L believe that very many more fish come from the Atlantic seaboard to Montreal and to Toronto than before the provision was made, so that I think the minister is to be * congratulated upon having continued the good work which was commenced by his predecessor. I realize that it is a most difficult matter to arrive at a fair finding regarding the seasons for fishing. The Fishery Board took upon itself to recommend the cutting down of the season in some districts to a greater degree than in others, and the department acted on their recommendation. The finding of the Marine and Fisheries Committee of this House was, I think, that the season should be reduced by a number of days in the very large districts, but, as regards one district, they amended that by declaring that after a certain year a further reduction in time would be made. I should like to tell the minister that the arrangement has been found to be burdensome. I do not think it is fair, for the season is too short. It is over almost before you know where you are.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: To what district does my hon. friend refer?

The district in the gulf of . the St. Lawrence, round a certain portion of Prince Edward Island, and between Coeagne on the New Brunswick coast and Pictou. The shortness of the season makes it difficult to operate the fisheries profitably.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I think the season in that district' extends from about the 20th or 25th of April to the 25th of June.
I thought it was up to the 1st of July.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I think it is up to the 25th of June. Does my' hon. friend think the season ought to be extended into July?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: What is the condition of the lobsters, with regard to their shells, at that time?
In my judgment, up to 10th of July the lobsters are perfectly good. We do not see the soft shell lobster on that coast until the month of August.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The season was fixed on the recommendation of the Shell Fisheries Commission. That commission took evid-

ence all along that coast from a number of people, and their belief was that if fishing were allowed after the date mentioned-I think it is the 26th of June-the lobsters would be taken at a time when their shells were soft. I have a very great respect for my hon. friend's opinion in regard to fishery matters, and to many other matters, but it evidently differs from that of the Shell Fisheries Commission. It is an in. stance of the difference of opinion there is among those engaged in the fishing business or interested in fishing. In my experience, I have found it a very difficult matter to get people to agree with regard to the length of the season. No matter what you fix, even after the most careful inquiry, you are bound to find criticism. I thought that, having gone through that district, and taken evidence, the Shell Fisheries Commission would be able to reach a correct conclusion, but apparently my hon. friend, who is so well informed in these matters, does not agree with them. It is an instance of the difficulty a minister has to encounter in. fixing the seasons.

I was present at a meeting of the Shell Fisheries Commission in the district I have reference to, and there was no such evidence as that given, so far as my memory serves me. I know from personal experience that there are no soft shell lobsters up to the end of July. What I find fault with is that the Shell Fisheries Commission, while proposing to reduce the season by a number of days all around the coast, which seemed to be fair, they made a special exception of a certain district, in which they said after' a certain date they would reduce the season still further. So far as 'I see it is not fair, because the season is so short that the fisheries cannot be operated properly.

Perhaps the hon. minister will find that out for me; I may have been

At any rate the arrangement is considered burdensome, and if the minister can see his way clear to remedy the condition, he should do so. speechtext: I think the Shell Fisheries Commission made a recommendation that the date should be the 26th June, and they also recommended a size limit. I do not think they could pack lobsters in certain districts if they insisted on a size limit. On the outside coast they might, but I do not think that in the bays of Prince Edward Island they could. They certainly could not around the districts where you continue the season well into the summer. The Ibbsters are very much smaller down there than they are in our district. At any rate, I think the matter is worthy of consideration. I think the minister really ought to change the finishing date to the first of July.
