The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

When the committee rose at six o'clock the hon. member for Northumberland was speaking about the close season for lobsters in different parts of the Maritime Provinces. In our district, the season used to extend up to the 15th of July, but a year or two ago, on the recommendation of the Shell Fish Commission, tire season w$s shortened to the



1st of July. Gloucester county, as the minister knows, is perhaps more interested in the lobster fishing industry than any other district in the Maritime Provinces, and I think that in order to encourage the industry it would be well for the department to consider changing the open season. For instance, in May .and June the fishermen along the coast of New Brunswick get very few really good fishing days, find I have always tried to impress upon the department, and particularly upon the can-ners, that it would be very much better to have a short open season in the spring, and another open season in the fall, from about the middle of August on as long as conditions permit. Naturalists say that the lobster is always in a healthy condition in the fall. In fact, the quality of the fish is better then than in the spring; it is larger, and would make a better showing in the can. The objection to this plan comes from the large operators, who say they would be put to the expense of putting their fishing gear out twice. I do not see much force in that. When the Shell Commission was at Bathurst two or tfiree years ago, I made it a point to be present, and gave my opinion on this matter. Whetner my suggestion has been looked into I cannot say, but certainly it has not been acted upon. I wish the minister would seriously consider this suggestion of mine. If the large iirms did not want to take advantage of the rail season as well as the spring, they could please themselves; but I submit that it would be to the advantage of the fishermen and can-ners to have the regular open season in the fall, and a short open season in the spring as wen.

I wish to say a few words along the line taken by my hon. friend from Gloucester. The season in our district opens on the 25th of May, and, extends to the 10th of August. Just ajoout the time the season opens, and after the fishermen have got their traps out, almost invariably there comes a heavy storm, and ice coming down the straits does great damage to the fishing gear. The fishermen, however, say tlhat the season is short, .and they put their traps out as soon as the season opens, taking chances of its getting damaged. The Shell Fish Commission considerec^ the whole business thoroughly a year or two ago, and, perhaps, they reported on this difficulty. I am not concerned very much about the man who sells the fish. The fisherman who catches it is who I am thinking of; She is the poor

man, and in his anxiety to get all the fishing days he can, he takes chances of getting his gear damaged; he has to face the wind, and the waves, and the storm, and when he has caught the fish, in many cases he has to sell it at a very small price indeed. It is the fisherman who gets the worst end of the deal with the canners. Furthermore, the packing houses start to operate about the 25th of July, and just about that time the lobsters are soft shelled; the quality of the fish is not nearly so good as later in the fall. It does seem to me that it would be better to lhave the open season a little later on in the year, when the fish has re-shelled, and is in good condition. Of course, I know that many things have to be considered before making a change like this. The department must consider wftether it would be in the permanent interests of the lobster fishing industry. Fishermen would always be able to get a good catch in the fall, whereas very few fish can be caught around the 25th of May. The open season extends from that date to the 10th of August. Sometimes I know the department, in their generosity, extend the season for a few days, but that is on sufferance, and sometimes the permits come late and the people have their gear taken up, so that the extension is not of very much advantage.

I desire to call the attention of the minister to what seems to be an anomaly in regard to the lobster industry along Northumberland strait. It was a regulation a couple of years ago-and I think the regulation is in force still-that along the western coast of the island of 'Cape Breton the season opened about a week or ten days earlier than along the shortes of Antigonish, Pictou, and other points along the mainland westward. The regulation also provided that the fishermen on the western coast of Cape Breton island could continue fishing operations for a week or so longer than the fishermen at those points on the mainland that I have mentioned. In other words, they have an advantage of about fifteen days in fishing along the western coast of Cape. Breton island over the fishermen of Antigonish, Pictou, and Colchester counties, and points along the Northumberland strait westwards. As the minister is well aware, it is the same kind of lobster that is caught off the west coast of Cape Breton island as is caught off the west side of the Northumberland strait. It iseems rather anomalous

that the fishermen of Port Hood or Creig-neish in the county of Inverness can have fifteen days longer fishing than the fishermen of Havre Boucher in Antigonish county, a distance of about twelve or fifteen miles directly opposite. The fish frequent the very same waters, and the same conditions prevail along the western coast of Cape Breton island as along the coast of Antigoniish county. What is the object in passing such am extremely absurd regulation? I am told it was done at the suggestion 'of the Fish Committee. If so, it does not justify the existence of that committee.
I also wish to ask the minister why it was that last year, when the fishermen of the counties I have just mentioned asked for an extension of the season, their request was not granted. As the minister knows, on account of ice conditions last spring it was well on to the 24th of May before the fishermen were able to get their traps out. Some of them had got their traps out a little earlier and were obliged to take them in, and those who did not take them in found them high and dry on the shore, driven in by the ice, so that they lost fifteen days at the beginning of the season. I think they asked an extension of only ten days, and it would seem that their request was a very reasonable one. If it were true that the water had got warmer as early in the season as it ordinarily does, and if it were true that the condition of the lobster had changed as early towards the end of the season as ordinarily happens, there would be some reason for refusing the extension as requested, but it seems to me that in the case which the fishermen presented, the department, if it gave this matter consideration at all, should have acceded to their request. It looks as if the department had not paid any attention to their request whatever, as if it had stereotyped rules, and as if it hdd carried them out regardless of the convenience of the fishermen.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I would like to express my appreciation of the spirit in which hon. gentlemen opposite have approached the consideration of the fishery Estimates, and of the moderate manner in which they have referred to matters of interest in connection with them. My hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair), who always takes a praiseworthy interest in matters affecting the fisheries of this country, has expressed a regret that I did not make a general statement about the work of the
149J
Fisheries Branch of the department. I would have been very glad to do so had I thought it would be desired, but I have followed the practice that has always been followed in connection with these Estimates. There are one or two departments whose ministers make a statement when their Estimates are brought down: the Railway Department and, I think, the Militia Department; but the practice in this department, ever since I have been minister- and I understand the same practice prevailed before I became minister-has been to give the information in regard to the various matters as the items come up. That is why it did not occur to ime to depart from the practice of previous years. I am anxious to give all the information I can to the committee, and any information that is wanted can be given as the different items are taken up.
My hon. friend from Guysborough referred also to the division of the department, and the assigning to the Department of Naval, Service of the Fisheries Branch which was previously carried on by the Marine Department*. The hon. gentleman is, of course, aware, I think I have explained this to the House on previous occasions although the hon. gentleman said he had never heard me do so-that there are two distinct departments over which I preside as minister, one the Department of Marine and Fisheries, the other the Department of Naval Service. Those departments, although under the same minister, are distinct departments and recognized as, such by the legislation which created them. When I came into the Government, the Department of Marine and Fisheries was administering the Canada Shipping Act and the very many things which that involved, the Fisheries Branch, the St. Lawrence ship channels, the harbours of Montreal and Quebec, and other harbours which are under a commission form of government and over which the Department of Marine has jurisdiction, the Meteorological Survey, and many other branches as well. The Naval Department was administering the Naval Act, the Hydrographic Survey, and one or two other similar branches. The result was that one department had too much to do and the other too little; and, after consultation with Mr. Johnston, Deputy Minister of Marine and Fisheries, and Mr. Desbarats, Deputy Minister of Naval Service who, at one time was Deputy Minister of Marine and Fisheries, it was decided in the interest of effective administration, of eonveni-

ence and of a proper dstributicm of the work, that more work should be given to the Department of Naval Service, and that some of the work assigned to the Department of Marine and Fisheries, which was overcrowded, should be taken away from it. For that reason, it was decided to take the Fisheries Branch from the Department of Marine and Fisheries and place it under the control of the Naval Service, and the result has been an equalization in the work of the two departments.
Mr. hon. friend has suggested that it is somewhat incongruous that the fisheries should be under the Naval Service. I do not think that is any more incongruous than that they should be under the Department of Marine and Fisheries. There is a branch of the Fisheries Department, the Fisheries Protection Service, which naturally falls under the head of the Naval Department because it is to all intents and purposes a naval service. It exists for the purpose of protecting our waters from the depredations that might be committed by fishermen of other countries, and for the purpose of keeping those fishermen outside of the three mile limit so that our fisheries may be preserved for our own people. That service requires ships, men on those ships, and guns on those ships, and is in a sense a portion of the naval service, of the country. All through the departments of the Government there are things which seem to be incongruous. For instance, why should the Department of Agriculture administer the Copyright Act and the Patents Act. One might think they more properly should come under the Department of Justice. The allotment is made for the purpose of equalizing the work of the different departments. When I came into the Department of Marine and Fisheries a question arose in regard to the ferries on the international rivers. I concluded at once that that was a matter for the Marine Department to deal with. But, to my surprise, I found that it was within the jurisdiction of the Department of Inland Revenue; though on what logical principle ferries -are put under the Department of Inland Revenue, I do not know. The same thing exists all through these departments. For instance, the Prime Minister has charge of the Mounted Police, which, it might seem at first blush, should be within the control of the Militia Department as the Mounted Police is -a force for the protection and defence of our people of our western country. It was for the pur-
[Mr. Hazen.j
poee, as I say, of equalizing the work in the two departments that the change was made. The hon. gentleman speaks as though the men whose business it is to deal especially with naval affairs have to deal with fishery questions. But, as a matter of -fact, the same men deal with the fisheries questio'n to-day as dealt with them before the change took place. The Superintendent of Fisheries, the Inspector of Fisheries, and other officers have been the same for many years. The only change is with the deputy minister. And, while the hon. gentleman refers to the fact that the Deputy Minister of Naval Affairs might not be supposed to have special knowledge of fisheries matters, yet the fact is that Mr. Desbarats was at one time Deputy Minister of Marine and Fisheries, and was taken from that position to fill the position of Deputy Minister of Naval Affairs. So he had many years of experience in the Marine and Fisheries Department before taking his present position. The result of the change has -been most satisfactory. Instead of having one deputy minister overworked and one department overworked, we have a fair division under which both deputy ministers-and they are very busy men-can do satisfactory work. And the fisheries officers who administer the Fisheries Act-the superintendent, the inspector, and the fishery experts-are practically the same men as before, and not the men who carry on the technical work in connection with naval affairs under the Naval Act. In other matters to which I have referred, the change has been conducive to the equalization of work and to efficiency, and has worked out most satisfactorily, as the hon. gentleman can learn if he will consult those who for years past, under my regime and under the regime of my predecessors, have been responsible for the technical work in connection with the Department of Marine and Fisheries.
The hon. gentleman has referred to the fact that there is an increase in the expenditure of the department since the change of Government took place in 1911. That statement is correct, except that the hon. gentleman to a considerable extent exaggerated what the increase has been. He said that it was practically doubled. He was not speaking by the book and evidently had not refreshed his memory by looking at the figures. This year, the estimate we are asking for Fisheries is $1,224,900. Now, I take the actual expenditure for the year 1911-12, which was $843,856. The present

Estimate shows -an increase over this actual expenditure of $383,044. The hon. gentleman is well aware that as. a rule the expenditure is not as great as the amount estimated; the difference in some years is very considerable.
It was the actual expenditure I gave.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
We have not the actual
expenditure for the current year yet. For the year 1914-15, the Estimate was $1,604,700, while the expenditure fell below that Estimate by about $300,000. As the Estimate for 1915-16 exceeded that for the present year by about $200,000, so the expenditure for 1914-15 exceeded that for 1915-16 by about $200,000. So, the hon. gentleman will see that during the last two years there has been a very considerable reduction in the expenditure of the department.
But Hhere are reasons, and very good reasons., too, why there was an increase in the expenditure. In 1911 there was a most incomplete organization of the fisheries in the western provinces. Commissions had been appointed prior to my coming into office to consider .and report upon that matter. The work of one of these had not been finished wtoen the present Government came into power. Following the reports that were received, the service was completely reorganized, and, in view of its previous incompleteness, a very considerable additional sum had to be spent. The provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan, and Manitoba were entitled to fisheries protection just as much as the rest of the country. That protection had not been accorded to them, and the lack of it had been recognized by the previous Government, who had appointed commissions to investigate and report as io what should be done. The jeorganized service was as complete as we could make it, and this added considerable to the expense of the department.
Then I take up the question of fish hatcheries. The policy of carrying on fish hatcheries was well under way in 1911. New hatcheries were being asked for in all directions.-new hatcheries are still being asked for, from the lakes, from the West, and from places, in the East. These institutions have done valuable work. I might refer to tlhe case of lake Erie, which, at one time, had been almost depleted, but is now fast coming back. The same is true of Georgian bay and lake Huron. Only the other day a delegation of gentlemen from lake Erie points, and members, of the House
on both sides who take an interest in the fisheries of lake Erie, urged upon me the establishment of a herring IbatcheTy on lake Erie, as they fearec^ the herring were being depleted, and there was a demand for all the herring that could toe produced. In 1911 we had forty-one fish hatcheries in Canada; others were undeT construction, and still others were promised. To-day we have sixty-one fish hatcheries. These have cost money to establish, and their maintenance also costs money. But I doubt if there is a member of this House who would suggest that this money has not been well expended, or that any of the hatcheries now in existence ought not to have been established.
Then we have the question of fisheries patrol. This service lhas been improved and is now reasonably complete. . The Fisheries Patrol service covers the fisheries lying inside the three-mile limit. For some years before I came into office, and since, the policy has been to enforce the laws by means of patrol boats. Five patrol boats were delivered, soon after I came into power, that had been ordered toy the previous Government, for wlhich we paid and [DOT] which we have had to maintain. We have now twenty-three patrol boats of our own on both coasts. A good many have had to be added in British Columbia, where the importance of the fisheries, is becoming greater all the time. The effect of ' this improved service has 'been much more complete protection of the fisheries. This is simply carrying out the policy of my predecessor. As I said, I found that five of these boats had been ordered before I came into power, and so had to be paid for, and every boat added to the service involves an additional amount for wages and maintenance. This year we are asking for a vote of $1,224,900. It is difficult to say how much of that will be spent. It may be that we will not come within $100,000 of the total vote, judging from our experience in other years. A good deal depends on what may occur during the year. Unless the decision of the court is given as to rights in tidal waters, that vote will not be employed. . If that decision is given in our favour then, we will at once have to take over the administration of the fisheries in the tidal waters in Quebec and the money here asked for, or a portion of it, will he required for that purpose. So it is with a number of the other items; hut we have reduced our Estimate by about $176,500 as compared with the Estimate of last year.

My hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) has referred to transportation in connection with fishery matters, and it is a very important question indeed. A policy was entered upon in about 1907 of paying a portion of the expressage on fish coming from the east and west to central Canada. That trade has increased very largely. The amounts we are paying now are very much larger than they were at that time. They increased, if I recollect correctly, until last year, when there was a slight decrease caused, my officers believe, by the fact that the fast freight service has become more efficient and fish that had previously been sent by express is now sent by fast freight. But that policy has given good results. Before the introduction of that policy, the markets of Montreal, Toronto and the large cities of Ontario were 'being supplied by fish from the United States. Those cities are now supplied practically entirely by fish from the Atlantic and the Pacific coasts of Canada, with the exception of certain fish that at certain seasons are found in the waters of the United States and not found in Canadian waters. The result of the policy ihas been that a great deal more Canadian fish is being used in the cities of Canada, and there is a very great chance,
I think, for further development. I understand from fish dealers in those cities that they are now selling more Canadian fish than they have done in the past, and that the exhibition in Toronto during the last few years has done a very great deal in that regard. Perhaps I might mention that last .year, in connection with the exhibition at Toronto, we were able to establish a fish restaurant, where an excellent fish dinner was served for 25 cents. Over 25,000 people were served at that restaurant, and those who had a dinner at it can testify to the excellence of the meals served. I had one myself, and I can vouch for its excellence, because I know something about fish. I am told by the fish dealers of Toronto that nothing has done so much to advertise the fisheries of Canada, so far as Ttoronto and western Ontario is ,concerned, as that restaurant.
What kind of fish did you have on the bill of fare?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
We had halibut, haddock, codfish, all fish that we could get that were in season. It was served in excellent condition.
Mil-. OOPP: Miratnichi salmon'5 IMr. Hazen]

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I think we had salmon from the Miramichi; we had salmon from both coasts. I hope that if the hon. member for Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) visits the Toronto exhibition this coming year-and it is well worthy of a visit at any time because it is, I understand, the largest annual fair held anywhere in the world-if he will go to the restaurant and gefi a fish dinner, I am sure he will be delighted with it, and ^ will agree that as a measure of advertising the restaurant was worth what it cost us.
And the minister made a very excellent speech.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I thank the hon. gentleman. We decided, after considering the whole question, that if we engaged cooks and waiters and everything and ran the restaurant ourselves, it would be. a very costly undertaking; so we made an arrangement with one of the largest restaurant keepers in Toronto, Mr. Naismith. We provided the fish and paid a portion of the rent of the restaurant, which' was the large dining-room under the grand stand. Mr. Naismith supplied the dinners at 25 cents each. Everything was served in a very cleanly and nice manner, and the result was that the restaurant was crowded at the mid-day meal; and sometimes three sets of meals had to be served, although it is a very large room. Was the price sufficient to pay the cost?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No. We provided the fish and we paid, I think, $1,000 for the other expenses. I think the restaurant cost us something over $3,000. With the experience we have had, it is probable that next year we will be able to run it more efficiently at a little less cost.

Were there any baskets left over?
Mr. HAZEN; No, I do not think there were any baskets left. In addition to that, we had an exhibit which was one of the most attractive features of the exhibition. We had the hearty co-operation in that exhibit of men who are engaged in the fish business in different parts of the country, and the large fish companies. The exhibit was a most attractive one and we were awarded the gold medal of the society for it. The year before, when I was at the exhibition I suggested to Mr. Oliver, the Pre-

sident of the Exhibition Association, that it might be a good thing to have a fisheries day, similar to their farmers' day, educational day, children's day, and so on. That suggestion was acted upon and they had a fisheries day at the exhibition this year, when everyone at the luncheon talked fish and fish was advertised and talked about in every way. I think the whole thing has proved an excellent object lesson. '
I think that out transportation policy has justified itself. The very fact that those cities were formerly supplied with their fish from the American waters and are now supplied entirely from our own waters, fully justifies the policy that was entered upon at that time. I am not satisfied with the service that the express companies 'have [DOT]rendered, and neither is the Department of Fisheries. This subject has been very fully and faiiriy discussed by the Marine and Fisheries Committee, to whom was referred the resolution of the hon. member for Digby (Mr. Jameson) and I presume when the report of that committee comes before the House lit will contain recommendations of a character which it may be possible io carry out and that will effect an improvement in the service. My hon. friend nas also referred to the question of improved communication with the United States, a very important question particularly, for the people on the south shore and the southeastern portion of Nova Scotia, from which my hon. friend comes. From our province a good deal of fresh fish goes to the Boston market in the summer on the boats operating between St. John and Boston. I understand that very large quantities of fish are also sent on the boats from Yarmouth to Boston. The suggestion, of my hon. friend is that something should be done to provide transportation from ports farther east. I understand that from many points on the south shore, with the railway communication that now exists fish is shipped via Yarmouth to Boston. Of course there are some points east of Yarmouth too far away from that city to make it easily possible to ship fish by that route. It is undoubtedly desirable that there should be steamers running from some of these points to Boston, and if it had not been for the conditions caused by the war, I understand that there would have been a line of steamers running now. I understood the hon. member for Shelburne and Queens (Mr. McCurdy) to say that an arrangement had been made whereby a private company
intended to put on a line of steamers running from a port there to the American market, but that in consequence of their financial arrangements being disturbed by the outbreak of war, they had not been able to consummate the scheme. I hope it will not be long before there are boats running in that direction. We have now free admission of fish to the markets of the United States, and it seems to me that it might be taken advantage of by private enterprise. It was with that intention, I believe, that the company, referred to by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queens in the discussion on the evening of the disastrous fire when the resolution of my hon. friend from Digby (Mr. Jameson) was before the House, was formed.
This afternoon and evening we have heard a good deal of discussion about the seasons for the catch of lobsters. That is a most difficult question to deal with. Hon. gentlemen all know that, years ago, lobsters were extremely plentiful all around the coasts of the Maritime Provinces. I remember that only a few years ago I was at the summer residence of Mr. Haszard, then premier of Prince Edward Island, and he told me that he remembered, not so many years bsEore, when* he could go out and with a hook in the afternoon, when the tide was out, from under the rock pull lobsters in sufficient numbers to fill a basket in a few hours. The same condition existed in numbers of places along the coast, but, in consequence of the great demand for lobsters, and of the canning of them for the markets of Europe and elsewhere, they cannot be obtained so easily to-day. The lobster fishermen have to set their traps further out than in years gone by. If there were no laws for the taking of lobsters, I think it will be admitted that the lobster would soon cease to exist. The question that faces any fishery officer, or any one charged with the responsibility of making and enforcing fishery laws, is, what laws can you pass which, while causing the minimum of interference with the trade carried on by the fishermen, will conserve the lobster supply for future generations as a source of wealth and industry. That proposition, as I have said, is a very difficult one to deal with. It is undesirable to pass laws providing the same close season for every part of the coast. You must have different seasons, having regard to the different conditions that exist; and it is in consequence of that that, here and there along the coast where you have a dividing line, people on one

side take the view that they are not being treated with the same fairness us people on the other side of the line. You must have a division somewhere. You must have some point marking a Change of districts and' that being the ease, there will always be- more or less friction between those on one side of the line and those on the other side. That is a state of affairs which cannot be prevented, I think hon. gentlemen will agree, under any system that can be devised.
My hon. friend from Northumberland (Mr. Loggie), whose views on any fishery matter are entitled to the very greatest possible respect, has referred to a district in which he says the season, which ends on the 26th of June, should be extended for a longer period. When I came into office in 1911, and discussed this matter with the Superintendent of Fisheries, and others, they pointed nut that, a good many years ago, there had been a lobster commission. I think the late 'Colonel Tucker and Mr. Bowers of Digby were members. The officers of the department thought that the conditions had changed somewhat since that commission had reported, and that it was desirable to have another commission to investigate the conditions. It was in consequence of these suggestions and reports that we appointed the lobster commission of which Professor Prince was chairman, and Mr. O'Leary, Ml. Wilson, and (Senator McLean were members. These gentlemen, after a very painstaking' investigation, after visiting points all along the coast, and holding meetings with the fishermen and others interested in the lobster trade, made a report which, to a considerable extent, has been acted upon, though not altogether. In the case of the district referred to by the hon. member for Northumberland, what they recommended was that the season should end on the 26th of June, and, in addition, that the size of the lobsters caught should be limited to eight inches. We did not give effect to the recommendation limiting the size to eight inches, and I understand that my hon. friend from Northumberland does not think it would be desirable to do so. We did shorten the season, making it end on the 26th of June, and if we had acted on their recommendation, we would have curtailed the rights of the fishermen to a still greater extent. My hon. friend from Gloucester (Mr. Turgeon) suggests that we should allow fall fishing. All these matters are worthy of consideration, but, so far as I am aware, no fall fish-
ing for lobsters has been allowed in the Maritime Provinces for many years past, if at any time, except at the Magdalen Islands. I believe that fall fishing was allowed in the Magdalen Islands, but the regulation which gave that right was rescinded before I became Minister of Marine and Fisheries. What the hon. gentleman says-that the lobster should be caught earlier in the season, that there should be a close period during the time that he is shedding his shell, when the shell is soft, and when he is not in good condition for canning, and that then, when that season is over, the fishing should go on.. If you allow lobsters to be caught in the spring and fall, you are going to catch lobsters which would otherwise breed and produce other lobsters, and there would be a danger of reducing the lobster supply. At any rate it is years since fall fishing was allowed, and the officers in the department, and the different commissions and those who have studied the question have been opposed to allowing fall fishing. I understand that the result of fall fishing in the Magdalen Islands was not of such a satisfactory character as to lead the department to continue it, and six or seven years ago they repealed the regulation, and prevented fall fishing there. My hon. friend from Antigonish referred to a question that arose there, and complained that I had declined to extend the lobster season last year. I have been endeavouring to prevent the extension of lobster seasons for the last three or four years. The regulations are made for the protection of the fishermen and for the protection of the industry. If you have regulations providing for certain seasons, during which lobsters are to be taken>
and the minister went to Council and got an Order in Council passed to extend the seasons, year after year, the matter would almost become a farce. These laws and regulations are made, as I have said, for the purpose of protecting the lobster fisheries. There is scarcely a year-and the district of my hon. friend is not exceptional in that respect-that petitions are not received asking for an extension of the season. Seasons are given that are plausible, that there have been heavy storms early in the season preventing the fisherman from get-ing out, that the ice continues to lie on the shores. That westerly winds had driven in the ice so that the fishermen could not get out, and so on. These are practically annual offerings, but I (have endeavoured to enforce the law in regard to the seasons,

and while I may have made errors, I would like to have the support of the members of 'this House who are interested in the fishing industry and in its preservation, in the course I have followed. During the last three or four years-the last three years especially-there have been scarcely any extensions in the fishing seasons, and while at first, perhaps, many fishermen thought it was not fair to them, I believe their opinion now is that it is a wise policy that tends to the preservation of the fish, and in the end will contribute very much to the advantage of the fishermen by enabling them to reap large harvests.
Are there no regulations as to the size of the lobster that can be caught? There are such regulations in the state of Maine.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
There are regulations in some districts. In, the Bay of Fundy district there is a regulation that no lobster can be taken that is under ten and a half inches. In that district there are no lobster factories. The lobsters which are caught are all sent fresh to the market-
* to a considerable extent, I believe, to the Boston market-and the fishermen are in favour of the regulation, because they believe it is in their interest, and there are no canning factories to interfere with it. But there are lobster districts so situated that the fishermen can not send their lobsters fresh to the markets in cities, or anywhere else, and to deprive them of the right of canning lobsters would be to take away, to a very Considerable extent, their source of livelihood and to interfere with what, for instance, in Prince Edward Island, forms a very important industry. Along the shore of Nova Scotia there are a great many canneries, extending from Halifax westward, where I hope in a few years the .fishermen will find it to their advantage to send their fish to the markets in a fresh condition. It will be better for them to do that than to sell their fish to the canneries, and the canneries will, I trust, in time disappear. In consequence of the conditions along that coast there is no size limit, but the season is a comparatively short one. There are different regulations for different districts, having regard to the conditions that exist. To come back to the question of the regulation of the fisheries, let me say that I am speaking in all candour. The whole discussion has been conducted in that mood, and I think that hon. members are desirous of helping this indusutry. It is not an easy thing for any minister to refuse these petitions. Pressure is brought, petitions come in, members of Parliament write to the minister, and that is what caused me once to say in the House that I almost wished that these seasons were a matter of statute, so that 9 p.m. the minister could not interfere, instead of being a matter oi regulation. Yet, I appreciate the fact that there might be in a particular year some very exceptional circumstances when it would be desirable that power should be vested in the Governor in Council to extend the season.
Mr. WM. CHISHOLM: Will lthe -minister explain the anomaly that (I pointed out?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
There is a district off Inverness in which the fishermen, as I understand the matter, fish for a longer season than they do in the district to which my hon. friend from Antigonish refers. If I remember correctly, the season in the district to which my hon. friend refers, and in the Northumberland straits, ends on the 26th June, and in the Inverness district it ends on the 15th July. I understand that in the latter district the prevailing winds are from the west and that keeps the ice in during the early part of the season to such an extent that the fishermen are not able to go out and set their traps. If the fishermen in Inverness were not given a longer season than the fishermen in the district to which my hon. friend refers they would not be able to catch any lobsters at all. The prevailing wind from the west blows the ice in on the Inverness shore to such an extent that the fishing is late and there would be no fishing at all if the season ended as early as in the district to which the hon. member for Antigonish refers. My hon. friend from Westmorland (Mr. Copp) referred to something of a similar character.
Mr. "SINCLAIR:	Will the minister tell
us from what source he got that informa-, tion about the difference in weather conditions along the Antigonish and Inverness coasts?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That information -was given to me by the officials of my department and it is also contained in the report of the Shell Fish Commission

The conditions east of St. George's Bay are precisely the same as they are west of St. George's

Bay. There is only one hay with Cape St. George on the one side and Port Hood on the other. Why make the distinction?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: You are airways going to have contiguous to the dividing line between districts some complaint of that sort but you have to make your dividing line somewhere. The people east of the line will think they do not have the same rights as the people west of the line and vice versa.
When was the season limited to the 26th June?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I think it was in 1913. In regard to the matter referred to by the hon. member for Westmorland, the season there commences on the 25th May and ends on the 10th August but wihat my hon. friend says is that the fishermen get no advantage by reason of its commencing on the 25th May because of the ice conditions there. But my hon. friend will see that the season extends to the 10th August which is a longer season than in many other districts. In the district referred to by the hon. member for Northumberland the season ends on the 26th June. It ends on the 10th August in the district of Westmorland and I think it takes in a part of Cumberland county too. The Shell Fish Commission recommended doing away with that and making it the 'Sanaa as in Northumberland, the 26th June. I concluded, after carefully considering the .matter, that if that were done, the fishermen would get feiw if any fish at all, and as the fish are in good condition in that district up to the 10th August, I thought it would be a fair thing to continue the season and I declined to act upon the recommendation of the iShell Fish Commission. It is not an easy question to deal with, and the only thing we can do is to get the best information we can on the subject, and-then use our best judgment. I can assure my hon. friends that the suggestions which they have made, and all in good part, will receive every consideration by the department.

I quite appreciate the difficulties of the Department of Marine and Fisheries in fixing the open season for lobster fishing in the Maritime Provinces. I do not suppose a more difficult subject comes before the department than this one. I do not mean to suggest that hon. gentlemen have not grievances with respect to the fishing situation in their respective constituencies, but I do know that it is extremely difficult to adjust the season to the satisfaction of all fishermen. To that extent I desire to give my support to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries when he asks for the co-operation of the members of this House.
I was very much interested in the minister's. statement of the efforts that were made at the Toronto Exhibition to place the prol

ducts of our fisheries before the people of Canada. The price charged at the lunch he spoke of was very reasonable, and if only the Minister of Railways would follow on the Intercolonial dining cars the example set by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries I am quite, sure there would be an increased consumption of fis'h all along that line of railway. The price charged at the Toronto Exhibition, according to the minister, was 25 cents each; number oi meals served, 25,000, making a total income of $6,250. There was a loss of $1,000, so that the. cost of supplying the fish to
25,000	people was $7,250.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Oh, no. The 25 cents included the whole luncheon.

Oh, I see. I may say that the Intercolonial charges 50 cents for a helping of fish in its dining oars; that is for the fish alone, not the whole luncheon. Fish in the county of Richmond and Guys-borough can 'be bought from the fishermen at 11 cents a pound, and the Department of Railways and Canals charges its patrons about $2 a pound for it. I do think the price charged on the Intercolonial for our own product is altogether unreasonable and extortionate. The Department of Marine and Fisheries is making an honest effort to increase the consumption of fish in all parts of Canada, but there is very grave complaint among, the patrons of the Intercolonial at the price they have to pay for the paltry helping of fish they get in the dining cars on that road. It is entirely out of proportion to the cost. This may be regarded as a small matter, particularly by hon. gentlemen who do not patronize the Intercolonial very frequently, but it is a very serious matter for the patrons of the road, who are not always in a position to pay a high price.
In respect to the increase in the cost of administering the Department of Fisheries at the present time as compared with the cost a few years ago, I have a specific instance having relation to the payment of salaries of fishery officers and inspectors and their gravel and outlay in the years 1912 and 1915. In the year 1912 Mr. A. C. Robertson, inspector of fisheries for western Nova Scotia, received a salary of $700, and his travelling allowance and outlay amounted to $975, making a total for the year of $1,675. For the year ended March 31, 1915, Mr. Ward Fisher, inspector of fisheries, who succeeded Mr. Robertson, received a salary
of $1,420.84, and for travelling allowance and outlay a sum of $3,424.69.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Let me correct my hon.
friend. That statement is absolutely incorrect in the Auditor General's Report; the mistake was made in the Auditor General's Office. If the hon. gentleman will look at yesterday's Hansard, he will see where the question was asked me if it was correct, and I stated it was not correct and I gave the correct figures. It is only fair to say that to my hon. friend so that he will not be misled by the figures an the Auditor General's Report.
The amount paid to Mr. Ward Fisher for travel and outlay included, I believe, the salaries of all the fishery guardians.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.

And all the travel and outlay which pertained to the discharge of their duties in respect to fisheries. Therefore when I state that the travel and outlay of Mr. Ward Fisher amounted to $3,424.68, I do not wish to imply that that was the travel and outlay of Mr. Ward Fisher alone; that includes also the salaries of the fishery guardians and their travel and outlay as wrell, so that while it would probably be incorrect to state, as is stated in the Auditor General's Report, that this large amount of $3,424.68 is made up of Mr. Fisher's travel and outlay alone, nevertheless it is an actual expenditure in relation to the administration of that fishery district. In addition to that Mr. Ward Fisher was supplied with a stenographer who received a salary of $455. As I stated a moment ago, Mr. Robertson's salary was $700 and the travel and outlay for the fishery guardians in that district amounted to $975, making a total of $1,675, whereas, the amount expended in Mr. Ward Fisher's regime was $5,300.52. The total, expenditure for the province of Nova Scotia during the year ended March 31, 1912 was, for salaries of four inspectors $3,820; for travel and outlay, $2,068.24, or a total of $5,888.24; the total expenditure in that province for the yeaT ended March 31, 1915 was, for salaries and outlay, $14,121.22, or an increase of $8,232.98. I scarcely think that any justification can be found for such a large increase. In the piping times of peace and plenty that existed in this country up to the 31st March, 1912, the total amount paid for administration of this branch of

the service in Nova Scotia was only 85,888.24, whereas during the lean period which succeeded the advent to office of my hon. friend's opposite the expenditure increased to 814,121.22. Let us see how this increase is made up. Mr. Robertson's salary was 8700; Mr. Ward Fisher's salary is 81,420.84, an increase of 100 per cent. The amount paid for outlay during Mr. Robertson's time was $975; the amount paid for during the year ended March 31, 1912 was, Fisher was in office was $3,424.68, or an increase of nearly 400 per cent. In addition to the very handsome salary paid to Mr. Ward Fisher, he has the services of a stenographer at a salary of $455 a year. Is the fact that Mr. Ward Fisher was a,candidate of the Conservative party in the province of Nova Scotia in the provincial elections of 1912 an explanation of the very large increase in salary he received when he was made Inspector of Fisheries? It is too bad that the Department of Fisheries should be regarded as a haven to provide safe rest and ease for political derelicts and castaways that are to be found throughout this country. The work that Mr. Ward Fisher has done, during the last year is not, I am sure, more effective nor important than the work done by Mr. Robertson during the year ended March 31, 1912. I do not quote these figures for the purpose of endeavouring to score a point against the minister on the ground of extravagance as much as to point out to him that at this period, above all others, there should be an honest effort made towards economy rather than towards increased expenditure. Every minister having estimates before this committee during the present session has expressed his willingness and determination to economize to the greatest possible degree in view of the large expenditure that this country has undertaken in connection with the war, but those professions in favour of economy on the part of Cabinet ministers -are no more than the expression of pious resolves on their part which are not given effect to.
With regard to the criticism made by my hon. friend from Guysborough that it was an unwise thing to attach the Fisheries Branch to the Department of the Naval Service, I desire to reiterate the criticism. The fisheries constitute a distinct and important industry in the Maritime Provinces and in western Canada. I think that industry is so important that it ought to he given a department designated by its own

name. The objections to that procedure stated by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries do not appeal to me. One reason given is that there is a Fisheries Protection Service which would naturally fall under the control of the Naval Service. Be that as it may, let all the ships owned by this Government be placed under the control of the Naval Service; but, as I stated a moment ago, the fishing industry is sufficiently important to_have a separate and distinct department of its own. During the last few years the Department of the Naval Service has certainly not been overworked. Not a great deal has been accomplished in regard to that service, and if the sub-department of Marine were attached to the sub-department of Naval Service so as to constitute one branch of the department and the Fisheries service another branch of the department, it would be a more logical and reason- . able division of tire work that belongs to those departments than the division in force at the present time.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
My hon. friend from Richmond referred to a statement in the Auditor General's Report. In order that no other hon. member may fall into error in consequence of that statement, and base an argument on it, I want to read the question and answer given in the House yesterday, as reported at page 2395 of Hansard:
Mr. Hartt:
1.	Referring to the following extracts from the Auditor General's Report for 1914-15, pages R-45 and R-46 : Inspector Morrison, travel and outlay, $4,023.14; Inspector Fisher, travel and outlay, $3,424.68 ; Inspector Hockin, travel and outlay, $2,527.87 ; and Inspector McLeod, travel and outlay, $2,857.93.
2.	Were these amounts actually paid for the purposes shown?
Mr. Hazen:	The amounts charged against
these inspectors in the Auditor General's Report do not represent the true amounts expended for them by travel and1 outlay. The Audit Office must have included other amounts not properly chargeable to expenses under this heading.
There is this further question and answer:
Mr. Hartt:
1. Referring to the following extracts from the Auditor General's Report for 1913, page O- 143, where the travel and outlay of Inspector of Fisheries D. Morrison, of Newcastle, N.B. are shown as $214.29, and at page O

144,' the travel and outlay of Inspector Ward Fisher, of Shelburne, N.S., are shown as $999.43 ; those of Inspector R. Hockin, of Pictou, N.S., as $599.33, and those of Inspector A. G. McLeod, of Whitney Pier, N.S., as $615.35; and at page R-45, of the Auditor General's Report for 1914-15, the travel and outlay of Inspector Morrison are shown as $4,023.14 and at page R-45, those of Inspector Fisher as $3,424.68 ; those of Inspec-

tor Hockin as $2,527.87, and those of Inspector McLeod as $2,857.93.
2. Why were these large increases necessary?	.
Mr. Hazen:	The amounts shown in the
Auditor General's Report for 1914-15 are incorrect, as the amounts actually expended by these officers in 1914-15 for travel and outlay are as follows : D. Morrison, $668.32 ; Ward Fisher, $1,236.43; R. Hockin, $609.42; A. G. McLeod, $567.47. The figures given in the Auditor's Report are greatly in excess of the above, and a serious mistake was evidently made in the Auditor General's office.
Apparently mistakes are made even in the office of the Auditor General.

Is it not the fact that these accounts include the salaries of fishery guardians and their travel and outlay? I moved for papers in the Public Accounts Committee.
' Mr. HAZEN: The figures appear there, and anybody would conclude that Mr. Morrison's travel and outlay were $4,023.14, whereas it was $668.32. There are a lot of other expenses which have been added in by the Auditor General.
Is there any other charge elsewhere in the report of the Auditor General for fishery guardians?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: If not, there ought to be.
The Auditor General simply included them in the expenses of the inspectors.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: He made a mistake and a wrong impression has gone abroad from these figures. I have letters from different parts of the country, including some from the inspectors, asking me how these figures were made up. The mistake has been made in the office of the Auditor General where other charges have been added in besides those of these men.
I so stated.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Any one reading that report would, conclude that these amounts had been paid out to these inspectors. I had a letter from one of them to-day. He said: I only got $600, and I am charged with over $4,000. It is a mistake that, to my mind, should not have occurred, but it did occur through some carelessness or oversight in the office of the Auditor General.
The hon. gentleman has referred to the salary paid to Inspector Robertson. He was paid the lowest salary of any inspector in Nova 'Scotia, though inspector for an important district. The fault was his own
-his own inefficiency. He was suspended on several occasions before I came into office, because he was not discharging his duty efficiently. Had he been efficient he would have been paid the same salary as the others-the several inspectors now receive $1,400, except Donald Morrison. The others are allowed clerks, as it was thought desirable that as these men are away from their offices a great deal of the time they -should have somebody to answer correspondence. Mr. Morrison, I understand, makes an arrangement with his daughter who does the same work for him as would be done by a clerk. Hon. gentlemen know that as time goes on there is more and more correspondence-there are more typewriters, more stenographers, abroad in the land, and if people's letters are not answered promptly by Government officials it causes vexation, and in some cases will cause a great deal of loss. The men appointed to these positions should give their whole time to the service, and for competent men who give their whole time the amount paid is not too large, having regard to the cost of living. In the second place, it is necessary that they should have clerical assistance, so that the affairs of office may be attended to. Unless an inspector is absent from his office a good deal he is not doing his work, because his business is to go about and see what is going on; the more he travels about the more efficient he is as an inspector. Mr. Robertson's salary was $700, which is a low salary, but this is not the fault of the department. It was really his own fault, because he was inefficient and did not attend to the duties of his office. As to Mr. Fisher, it is true he was a candidate for a seat in the Legislature of Nova Scotia. But that is not, to my mind, a discredit, and I do not think it should debar him from holding an office under the Crown. The officials to whom he is responsible find that he has proved an admirable official; he is capable, active, and intelligent, a most excellent inspector. The fact that he has been a candidate, as I say, should not debar him from holding office. If you go through the department in Ottawa you will find many officials who have been candidates for office and who were appointed by the previous Government. There is no reason why they should not be appointed, as there is no reason why Mr. Fisher should not be appointed because he has been a candidate for the local legislature before he entered upon the office which he now holds and in

which he has made good and has given every satisfaction to his superiors.

I have no fault to find with
Mr. Ward Fisher, and I raise no objection because he was a candidate. But I do say that the fact that a man has been a candidate of the Conservative party does not entitle him to special treatment with regard to salary and expenses.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: He is getting the same as the other inspectors.

I desire to reiterate what 1 said. I did not say that Mr. Ward Fisher's personal travel and outlay was $3,424.68. I stated that that included the salaries of the fisheries guardians in his district with their travel and outlay as well. There is no difference of opinion as to what we are talking about. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries would desire to convey the impression that the figures given by him include all the expenses in connection with these districts. But I give the information as I have it from the Department of the Auditor General. I was astonished to learn that there was a charge of $3,424.68 for travel and outlay by Mr. Ward Fisher, and moved for the papers in the Public Accounts Committee. I found that this charge was made up, not only of his own travel and other outlay, but, as I said, of the salaries of guardians and their outlay as well. So the statement I made at the beginning is absolutely true, that whereas the total amount paid in 1912 to the inspector of fisheries and for all the salaries of the guardians and their outlay as well was only $1,675, the amount paid in Ward Fisher's district for his salary and the payment of salaries of his guardians amounted to $5,300. The same thing is true with regard to the other figures I gave, so that the Minister of Marine can not minimize the _ force of my criticism by stating that the Auditor General improperly charged up to the inspectors all this outlay, which was made actually by guardians. That makes a total amount, which, in both cases, includes the salaries of inspectors, their personal outlay and salaries, of guardians in Nova Scotia for the year ending March 31, 1912, of $5,888.24, and for the year ending March 31, 1915, of $14,121.22. I took up this matter when the papers were brought down, and I found that there was no error in the report of the Auditor General, except that he did not specify that part of this item for travelling allowances of in-
speotors should be travelling allowance for guardians. But the result is. the same, and it totals as I said.

The minister said he would be glad to receive suggestions from members with reference to seasons in which lobsters could be fished in the Maritime Provinces. In the straits of Northumberland the season now ends on the 26th of June. Previous to coming to this House I was asked by a great number of fishermen to see the minister and to endeavour to get an extension of that season until about the 5th of July. Last yeaT, owing to ice conditions, the fishing did not commence until between the 10th and the 15th of June, and the consequence was that a great many fishermen were able to get but very few fish.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I wonder if in the last ten days they did not do as well as they would in a whole season in an ordinary year.

On the north and western portions they had good catches, but in the eastern end of the straits of Northumberland the catch was very poor. I do not know why the season was cut down to the 26th of June. I do not see any valid reason why it should be. The fish are just as good on the 5th of July as on the 26th of June. It is not because they are not as good, but for some other reason which the fishermen do not understand, and the opinion of all the fishermen in those sections of Northumberland strait is that the season should be so arranged that they should have a greater length of time to engage in fishing. In the western parts of the straits they have a better chance than on the eastern parts. When the east wind prevails the ice conditions are very very bad. The ice is caught on the north side of the island and is jammed into the Northumberland straits, and the consequence is that the fishermen have very little chance to fish. They cannot put out their traps while the ice is there. I believe the same condition prevails along the shores of the county of Antigonish. It did last year. I think the minister should take this into consideration. I know that the Shell Fish Commission made certain suggestions, but I do not think they were practical; at least the majority of them were rejected by the Government. I think the consensus of opinion among the fishermen is that the season should be extended in the eastern end of Northumberland straits until the 5th day of July.

I want to draw attention to what I think is a discrepancy. In the district referred to as starting on the 24th of May and ending on the 21st of August, they have 2 months and 17 days to fish, whereas in the other district that I made complaint about, beginning on the 25th of April they would have only 2 months and 1 day, if they fished every day. At S'hippigan island and around Biscoe point it is the rule that the factories do not get started until about the 15th of May, so they have a fishing season of only about 40 days, and the overhead charges of getting ready and waiting all of tliat time, if the ice conditions were adverse, renders the business unprofitable. So I think there is a good deal in what the hon. gentleman from Prince Edward Island has said. If you like, make the season four or five days later, but at any rate it should end about the 5th or the 1st of July, certainly not before the 1st of July. It might be better to have it end on the 10th of July as it used to.

OCajpe Breton North) I am pleased that the' discussion this evening has been of a somewhat practical character and not contentious. It is only about once a year that hon. gentlemen on the opposite side have an opportunity of talking to the minister about these matters, and it is not to be wondered at that we have something to say on the very important subject of fisheries, particularly those of us who come from fishing districts. I suppose the minister looks upon this ordeal of coming here with his Estimates as something to be dreaded.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Oh, no; it is very pleasant.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Is there no person down there in commercial life who will put up
a freezer and get the assistance authorized by the Government?
That has been a failure in the past there.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The hon. gentleman knows of the assistance the Government gives?

I am quite familiar
with it but it has been a failure, although that is no fault of the department. I am not blaming the Government for it, but I think the department has neglected their end of it. The freezers have fallen into the hands of private parties who are using them, without exception, in connection with their.own business and the fishermen have no further interest in them. What is absolutely necessary is that the whole thing should be under the control of some officers of the Government. The building should be erected by the Government, the fish caught by the Government, put in there and sold out as required-sold, of -course, as cheaply as possible, but the chief thing is always to have a supply on hand. It never will be a success unless the Government takes hold of it, establishes it properly, doing it at the least possible expense and in such a manner that there will be a constant supply of bait. There are tons and tons of this fish in the spring of the year. Catching it and putting it in would be very inexpensive, and all that would be necessary would be to look after the bait and give it out to the fishermen when required.

The minister spoke of fall fishing. I thought the natural inference from his remarks was that fall fishing was not allowed, but I suppose the minister would be very much surprised if I said that it was allowed. It has been allowed on certain coasts of Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick contrary, I am sure, to the minister's wish. But, as a matter of fact, the law has been disregarded. In certain sections of New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island fall fishing does go on illegitimately. Of course, it would hardly become me to be more personal than I have been.
If it were not for the fact , that
10 p.m. I do not believe the lobster industry can stand fall fishing, I would strongly recommend that fall fishing be allowed because it is absolutely unfair that the Government should allow the law to be broken when those who endeavour to protect the fishery and who obey the law close up their factories and go home. Other people along the coast, contrary to law, go



on with their business and it is very important, in the interest of the industry, that this illegal fishing be stopped. If the industry could stand it and all were allowed to fish for a month in the fall, it would be another question altogether. It seems to ipe that it is incumbent upon the department to see that illegitimate fall fishing is stopped. While I am on my feet, I want to say to the minister that the breakwater at point Sapin, Kent county, is sanded up so much that it is almost impossible to get lobster boats into harbour there. I am sure that thd local Public WTorks engineer has made a note of it and sent it to the department. Perhaps, in the interest of the fisheries, the minister will suggest to the Minister of Public Works that this work be done as early in the season as possible.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I will be glad to call the attention of my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers) to what my hon. friend (Mr. Loggie) says as to the necessity of some repairs to the breakwater at point Sapin. I understand my hon. friend is opposed to the fall fishing of lobsters?
I am opposed to fall fishing against the law.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
My hon. friend does not think it desirable that it should be permitted? In that respect he differs from the view entertained by the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Turgeon). I understand my hon. friend to say that there is illegal fishing going on in the fall. I am told by the officers of the department that they do not think there was any illegal fishing in New Brunswick last fall. If my hon. friend would tell me in confidence of any cases he knows of in which there has been illegal fishing, I will take very prompt steps to put a stop to it. We are dependent upon the zeal and energy of our officers to stop anything of that sort. The impression among the officers in my department who have to do with this matter is that' there is nothing like the amount of illegal fishing going on that there was in former years, and they believe that in New Brunswick last fall there was practically none at all. There may have been a few isolated cases. If my hon. friend could give me, for my own personal information, without making the matter public at all, any information on the subject, I would be very glad to have it. My hon. friend from Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) referred to the bait question. Of course, there is a provision now under which, if any one will, under certain condi-

tions, embark upon the erection of a bait freezer or warehouse, the Government will give him assistance to an amount not exceeding $2,000, and pay him a bounty of $5 per ton on the amount of bait purchased up to a certain quantity.
Apparently, from what my hon. friend says, that has not been sufficient to meet the case in the district he refers to. This is the first time I have heard the suggestion that the Government should [DOT] build these freezers and stock bait, and sell it to the fishermen from time to time. I believe it was in 1909 that this policy of assisting the fishermen was inaugurated, and it was thought it would be sufficient to meet the case. I believe advantage has been taken of the system to some extent.
I have a good knowledge of the freezers, and I can say that the policy has been a failure.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There would be some difficulty in the way of the Government building these freezers and stocking them with bait. They would have to keep men there all the time to sell the bait to the fishermen. The difficulties are not insurmountable, of .course, and the suggestion of my hon. friend will be considered.
You could get a local man to do the work very cheaply, without giving up his regular work.	[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It was hoped at one time that the fishermen would co-operate.
What is the season for lobster fishing on the north shore of Baie des Chaleurs. Has the season been changed lately?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There has been no change for some years. The season opens on the 26th of April, and ends towards the last of June.

Does the minister realize that the geographical situation along that shore is very different from the situation in Nova Scotia? Between Carleton Point and Miguasha Point there used to be a good lobster fishing ground, hut it has been practically closed down for the last few years. I have been in the habit of going to that district for the last fifteen years, and know it very well. An ice bridge forms every year between Carleton and Miguasha Points and the mainland; and on account of that, and the very short season, no fishing is done there now. Bernard Leclerc, who has been in the fishing industry for the last thirty years, had to

close down a year or two ago, owing to the peculiar conditions. He was never able to	in earlier than the very last
day of May, and sometimes the beginning of June, and the season closed at the end of June. He has repeatedly told me that fishing would be profitable at that point in September, but owing to the regulations of the department and the lateness of the season, they can get only about a month's fishing in the year. Conditions are not quite so bad as you go down the coast of Gaspe and Bonaventure, but I think a longer season should be allowed there.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I know there are difficulties at Carleton Point; the ice remains there pretty late in the season. Of course, it is difficult to fix the season to suit all parties.

I should have mentioned that the current of the Restigouche river passes along the New Brunswick shore at that point, and the channel is clear of ice at a very early period in the season; but on the north shore of the Baie des phaleurs conditions are as I have described. I should like to inquire whether the results , of the Port Daniel hatchery were satisfactory. Last year a heavy storm swept away part of the apparatus, and part of the wharf.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The results "were fairly satisfactory, though not as satisfactory. as we could wish. I will later give my hon. friend full information on this.
Has the lobster hatchery on the Gaspe and Bonaventure coasts been satisfactory? I understand not.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not think it is in a very good position. It has not been as satisfactory as other hatcheries.

I desire to emphasize the observations made by the hon. member for North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) with reference to bait. The late Government gave substantial aid. to bait warehouses in my county. I must say, however, that what has been done there has been rather discouraging. I do not know of any place in the county where bait is kept for any length of time in the year. In that respect the county of Inverness is circumstanced somewhat similarly to the county of Victoria. We have about 100 miles of cbast, and a large number of people dependent upon fishing; but, unfortunately, at certain seasons of the year they have great difficulty in getting bait to carry
150J
on their calling. I think the hon. member for Cape Breton has suggested the only practical solution of the bait problem in certain sections of the Maritime Provinces, and I have particularly in view Inverness county. We have a great many difficulties there. If the Minister of Public Works were in his seat I would call his attention to certain matters, but I will wait until his Estimates come up. Eight or ten years ago a number of artificial harbours were started there, but in the last three or four years no work has been done on them. Our fishermen are deprived of anchorage, and large numbers of them have abandoned fishing. I will have more to say on this point when the Minister of Public Works brings down his Estimates. But just now I particularly wish to endorse the suggestion of the hon. member for North Cape Breton with respect to bait. I know of no other solution of the question. Several places were opened up in the county of Inverness-four or five at least, I think- but they are all closed down. It is true that the fishermen showed very little interest. The policy was a good one, but the fishermen did not feel disposed to carry it out. At first they took a great deal of interest in these places, but they soon abandoned them entirely. Most of them are now closed down, or in the hands of private parties; so I do not hope for very much from that policy.

Early in the session the minister, replying to a 'question I put on the Order Paper with regard to the lobster season on the eastern side of the straits of Northumberland, said that ,the season had been fixed as a result of the report ol the committee who had considered the question. The situation is this: last year, owing to the prevalence of ice in the	gulf,	the	fishing season did
not begin until the 10th of May. The lobster traps were not put out until that date and the period being until the 26th of June, the fishing season continued for a period of only six weeks. The result was that there was a great deal of trouble amongst the lobster people, and some of them have gone out of business and sold their factories and others are considering doing the same thing if the season is to be limited to such a short period. The minister can readily see that, as he has fixed a beginning of the season and has also shortened it at the other end, in a season where the ice is very bad off the coast, the period

during which the, fishermen can do business is reduced to a minimum and, in consequence, people hesitate to expend money in engaging fishermen and laying in supplies on account of the risk of coming out losers on account of the restricted period during which they can fish. This year we have had a very severe winter. We are on the verge of the 1st of April, and great difficulty is being experience,by the winter boats in crossing-although the ferry to Prince Edward Island has done pretty well -and there is a tremendous quantity of ice off the coast. During the last week I have received letters pointing out that, if the season should be late in opening and the period of fishing should again be limited this year, the matter will be very serious. I am at a loss to understand why there should be such a marked difference in the season between the point at Malagash running east and the same point running west. It is quite right to restrict the fishing within a limited period; but, where you have conditions such as I have indicated, where you have a large number of men who are dependent for their income upon the fishing during that period, where you have capital invested, where you have people who go out in the winter time and prepare the supplies necessary for the fishermen, if the period on account of ice conditions is restricted to five or six weeks, the minister will see that it is restricted too- much. A number of really high class men are engaged in the business and they are anxious to see the industry preserved, but they feel that, if they are compelled to restrict their fishing operations within such a very short period their remaining in business will be interfered with. I see by the local papers that two men, whom I know very well, have sold out their factories; they are probably among the very best men in the business, and I see that one man who is a speculator has come into the business. In view of the conditions which resulted last year, I would ask the minister whether he would not consider this year, in the event of the season being late in opening-and it is very easy to find out when the people in that district run their lines-extending the season in order to avoid a loss to them. I understand the price of lobster is very high this year, and I do not think we ought to interfere with the opportunity these people have of making a livelihood. At the present time in Canada the production of all kinds of food, fish from the sea, wheat from the land, is of very great importance.
[Mr. Macdonald-1
Increased production.

Yes. I think the request is very reasonable, in view of the experience of last year. I know the complaint is not a captious one, but is based upon serious conditions that warrant a remedy, and I would ask the minister to endeavour to remedy the conditions last year.

I do not think the minister should have a cast-iron rule about the open season for fishing lobsters. I quite appreciate the position taken by my hon. friend from Pictou, because I know the condition of the fishing on his coast last year and on the coast of Antigonish County. I recollect being approached by a number of people who pointed out to me that the season had been so late that it was impossible to make ends meet and carry on their business unless some extension was given. I did not depend upon hearsay or on my own judgment in regard to these matters; the message 1 sent to the minister asked him to consult his officers.
