There is a staff of fishery officers along the coast who know the dates on which the fishermen set their traps, so that they have all the information and know the condition of the ice and the time that the season will last. They are the men who, if they are any good, ought to be able to answer that question. 1 do not know whether the minister is responsible for this or not, but there is a pretty general feeling that no request of this kind is listened to; that such requests are simply pushed aside and the cast-iron rule is that the department will not listen to any one. The department should listen to representations of this character and 'should be able to judge whether any concession should be made or not.
I think that illegal lobster fishing still goes on to a certain extent. Many people had hoped, when the minister employed patrol boats-and I [DOT] understand he has a number of them along the coast which are able to go rapidly from one point to another and which, I suppose, are costing us a great deal of money-that they would put an .end to illegal lobster fishing. In the town in which I live, lobsters are exposed in the windows for sale out of season; there is a trade going on in lobsters around that locality and no one seems to take any notice of it. If the minister will visit my town during the winter when the close season is on, I think I can show him places where he can purchase lobsters. I do not know to what extent this state of affairs exists

around the country, but I think it is pretty general, and I am afraid that the patrol boats and the staff which the minister has looking after the prevention of illegal fishing are not doing the work they should be doing.
I would also like to ask the minister if he would let us know the work that is being done by the Advisory Board. What use are they? What work have they done? On what questions have they given the department advice? Who are they and what do they cost us?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: First of all, with reference to the matter referred to by my hon. friend from Pictou and by my friend from Guys-borough, I will, of course, give consideration to recommendations made to me by those hon. gentlemen or by any others in respect to matters of public interest. The representation was made in good faith and should receive the very best consideration that the officials of my department and I myself are able to give it. I think it would be too soon to say to my hon. friends that the season will be extended. The matter will be watched. We will see what success the fishermen have, and if it is in the public interest that it .should be extended, I shall be glad to extend it. I may say that I am very loath to extend these fishing seasons, for reasons which I have given to the House, when I think the hon. gentleman was not then in his seat. The regulations have been framed for the purpose of protecting the interests of the fishermen perhaps more than any other class. If, after these close seasons have been defined with serious thought and on the fullest consideration of the facts, a change is made, unless that change is made for very strong reasons, the regulation simply becomes a farce.

But the minister
must take into consideration that the ice comes in.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The question arises in a
number of places that the winds hold the ice in near the shore so late in the season that it gives little fishing to the men. That is a reason that is to be considered, and when these petitions are in they will be considered very carefully. My hon. friend from Guysborough referred to petitions received last year, and I may tell him that we give full consideration to these petitions before dealing with the matters they refer to. We obtain reports from our fishery
officers, and consider them carefully; we do not come to a decision simply because of a cast-iron rule on the subject, but give full consideration to what is in the best interest of the fisheries and of the public.
My hon. friend has referred to some illegal fishing. I would say to all members of the House who are interested in the protection of the fisheries that any information they may give on the subject of illegal fishing will be regarded by me as absolutely confidential; for if the illegal fishing is going on and our officers are not alive to it, I should like to know of it that a remedy may be applied. The patrol boat system was introduced before I came into office. The man in the patrol boat ought to be in the best position to enforce the law against the illegal catching of lobsters. Of course, we may be mistaken, but the opinion we have formed in the department is that the patrol boat policy has been successful to a great extent. And while we do not say that, there is no illegal fishing-no doubt there will be illegal fishing as long as human nature is what it is-yet the belief in the department is that this patrol boat system, has greatly decreased the illegal fishing of lobsters, and that it is a very effective system.
Another point referred to by my hon. friend is his suggestion that lobsters were caught illegally, because he had seen them on sale in the town in which he lives during the close season, which would not be conclusive evidence of an infraction of the law.
They probably come from the south shore.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Yes, where the season
opens earlier. It is not against the law to send lobsters into a community where a close season for lobsters prevails. It may be that the lobsters the hon. gentleman saw were legally caught in a district in which the close season was different from that established in the district in which he lives.
The hon. gentleman has asked me to say a few words about the Advisory Board. The Advisory Board consists of the following:
For Nova Scotia, Messrs. W. 0. Smith, Lunenburg; H. B. Short, Digby; A. King, Halifax; G. A. Hemon, Shelburne.
For New Brunswick: Messrs. P. P. Russell, St. Andrews; F. T. B. Young, Cara-quet; A. B. Carson, Richibucto.
For Prince Edward Island: Mr. P. H. B. Longworth, Charlottetown.

For Quebec:	Mr. Azade Arsenault,
Grindstone, Magdalen Islands.
Mr. MARCH,: The mainland of Quebec is not represented. And there is no communication between the mainland and the Magdalen Islands. They are in the constituency of Gaspe, for Federal purposes; but Mr. Arsenault knows nothing of the conditions on the mainland.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It may be that there should be another member for that district, but I have given the membership of the board as at present constituted.
What were the expenses last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That question was answered. For the year 1915-16, the current year, the expenses have been $708.85. For 191415, the expenses for all branches of the board, including the Atlantic, the Central and the Pacific Committees, amounted to $3,676.
Are the members paid?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
They are paid $10 a day
when they attend meetings, and there are about two meetings a year.
Do they meet every year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Every year, and perhaps
twice a year. Their last meeting was in Charlottetown, the next, I understand, is to be held in Halifax.
Have they to do with fixing the fishing season?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
They discuss all matters
of that kind with the Department. Their duties are advisory; they have no administrative functions.
Can the hon. gentleman give a case in which the advice which they gave has been adopted?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
They have given considerable advice that has been adopted. They discuss matters with the fishery officers of the department, and these officers regard their advice as of great assistance, as they come from fishing communities and are in touch with the fishing business in the districts in which they reside. They enable the officers of the department to keep in direct and almost continuous contact with what is going on in the different branches of the fishing industry throughout the country, and their having such knowledge secures better administration. The amounts paid

to the members of the advisory board last year were:
Mr. Azade Arsenault, $132; Mr. W. G. Casey -I understand that he is the secretary- $225; Mr. G. A. Hemon, $50; Mr. A. King, $65; Mr. P. H. B. Longworth/ $40; Dr. E. E. Prince, who is a member of the board, $28.75-that is for travelling expenses; he would not be paid any fees-Mr. II. B. Short, $107; and Mr. W. C. Smith, $50. The total expenses for the year so far are $708.85. Of course, the amounts paid differ, because some members attend all the meetings and others do not. But the members get their travelling expenses and a per diem allowance of $10.
When did they meet last?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: In November.
How often did they meet last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The Atlantic division met once, the Pacific division twice.

Would it not be wise for them to meet in the spring rather than in the fall? A cast-iron rule, as referred to by the hon. member for Guysborough, is not always right, as the seasons vary so much. The Minister of Railways, at a time when we had spring weather in Ottawa, announced that the whole Metapedia valley was tied up with the worst storm of the year. The indications are that we are to have a very late spring on the Gaspe coast. If this Advisory Board sat in February or March, they could advise the department, and it would be a more valuable service to the fishermen, rather than to wait until the fall' when the operations are over.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: They are supposed to meet in April and November, but there are variations. These gentlemen give their time without remuneration, and their wishes and business engagements must be considered. They meet twice in the year, in the spring and fall.

Has the
minister any particular policy in respect to the location of the members of the board?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
There is no particular
policy except this: It was thought that, having regard to the importance of the fisheries, it would be well to have 4 members from Nova Scotia, 3 from New Brunswick,
1 from Prince Edward Island and 1 from the Baie des Chaleurs district; but there is nothing to say what part of the country

they shall come from. It is very desirable, of course, to have men representing different .phases of the industry. The gentleman from Halifax, Mir. King, was .appointed on the recomendation of the Board of Trade of Halifax. Mr. Smith is from Lunenburg. Mr. Short is a fish dealer at Digby. In New Brunswick, Mr. Young is from Caraquet shore, where there are a great many fishermen, and his life has been spent among them there. Mr. Russell is familiar with the fisheries in Passamaquoddy bay and part of the bay of Fundy, while Mr. Carson has a knowledge of fisheries along the Northumberland straits, the counties of Kent and Northumberland. Mr. Longworth, of Prince Edward Island, is an authority on the fisheries of the island. But if a vacancy occurred in New Brunswick, there is no policy as to what part of the province the successor should come from. If Mr. Carson hapened to drop out, there is no reason for his successor being appointed from Kent. We would try to get a man who understood the business well.

A very
large section, the eastern portion of the province of Nova Scotia, is not represented on this board. The island of Cape Breton is entirely surorunded by fishing coast, yet it has not one representative on the board. Two years ago I called the attention of the minister to this matter, and I think I got a promise from him that he would see to it that one at least would come from that portion of Nova Scotia. I am sorry to know that he has not carried out that promise.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I do not think I gave a
promise.
Mfr. WILLIAM! CHISHOLM:	But it is
a very very glaring condition of things. If the Board is of importance-and I think it is and can be of great service-it must be very striking to the minister that he should have abandoned the four counties of Cape Breton island where the largest proportion of fishermen of the province are to be found. It must (be clear to the minister that there is some method in this. The fisheries of Cape Breton island are important. The lobster fisheries are important, and the minister would be much aided by having a man from that portion of the country for the simple Teason that in certain years the season is late; the ice may remain on the bays for a month longer in one year than in the preceding year, and there are delicate questions for decision. A representative of the Board from
that portion of Nova Scotia would .aid the minister in carrying out his regulations and making the rules less stringent. The hon. member for Guysborough has characterized the rule as very stringent. I recognize that the Board will be of great aid (but it will be only if members are located in a practical way and they take an interest in their work. I venture the statement that no one of this Board knows the first thing about the fisheries of Cape Breton island, .and how -should they? The bon. minister tells us that one gentleman knows the deep sea fisheries and another is acquainted with the fisheries in general.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My information is that Mr. King of Halifax is largely interested in fisheries in Cape Breton.

I know the fisheries in Cape Breton but I never knew of Mr. King as a practical fisherman. I knew there was such a gentleman in Halifax, but I didn't know that he had any interest in the fisheries of Cape Breton. I am quite positive that neither be nor any other man on the Board ever put a foot on the coast of Antigonish with the knowledge of the fishermen. I assume the object of this Board is to aid the fishermen in every way possible, and that the members of such a Board, should be acquainted with the fishermen who would thus be enabled to communicate suggestions to them which the Board would bring to the attention of the Government. As it is now, in Cape Breton we have no connection with the Board, we know nothing about it at all.

There was a very
important slogan in our province at one time, "Justice to Cape Breton," and I want to bespeak that from my hon. friend now.

The minister says that he thinks illegal lobster fishing has decreased very much recently. I do not know that I will altogether say he is wrong in that, but I do say that it has increased since the new regulation regarding increase in license has been in force. Of course the minister is not responsible for that; I think the late Government put that regulation into force, and then illegal fishing started. It has perhaps not been so bad recently as it was two or three years ago. The attention of the department was drawn to a case some two years ago, when the lobsters were found in the packer's cellar, but that was the end of

it. I suppose the minister could not go any further.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
If they had the stamps
on-
They had the stamps on, as I understand, but that does not necessarily mean that they were not packed illegally.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Our officers now put the
*stamps on.

I did not say that the
officers put the stamps on.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I say that now the officers put the stamps on.

The objection I haye to the point made by my hon. friend is this: we have had some experience of that kind, and what happens is that the fish merchant will only sell bait to men who bring their fish to him, and in that way he creates a monopoly. There may be another merchant in the place who has no freezer, and if they sell their fish to that man, they will not get bait at all. The merchant says to the fisherman: "I will give you so much, and if you do not bring your fish to me you will get no bait." That is what happens in some districts that I know. If the Government owned a freezer, they would sell their fish wherever they' could get the best price.

I notice in the Auditor 'General's Report on page R-46 the salaries of different fishery inspectors. There are Inspectors Calder, Chapman, Harrison, Morrison and Robinson. Is Mr. Chapman still engaged by the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: His services are available for consultation, but he is practically superannuated.
I presumed that he had been superannuated. I would have no fault to find with that, as he is an old and competent official.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: He is a very old man.

But he is well preserved and has done excellent service for the department. I have no criticism to offer in that regard, but in regard to the man appointed in his place, Mr. Morrison, of Newcastle, I should like to point out that while Mr. Chapman's salary was $1,300 per year, with a travelling allowance of $441, making a.

total of $1,741, according to the Auditor General's report for 1915, Mr. Morrison's expenses amounted to $4,023.14.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It includes the expenses of some other people.

My hon. friend from Richmond (Mr. Kyte) referred to the fact that Mr. Ward Fisher had at one time been a candidate for the local legislature in the province of Nova Scotia, and asked the minister whether or not his appointment was given in return for the services which he had rendered to his party. I have no fault to find, with the present fishery inspector, Mr. Morrison. It was, I suppose, a case of making some return for the sacrifice he had made in the county of Northumberland. I have no fault to find with the appointment, but I do think that the increase in salary was rather unnecessary, because Mr. Chapman was a very competent officer. I am sure the minister will agree with me in that. No man could have been more competent than Mr. Chapman; the officers of the department will 'bear me out in that statement. I also noticed the name of Mr. Harrison, of Fredericton. He gets exactly the same amount as Mr. Chapman, and I suppose in the same position. I turn to the Auditor General's Report of 1915, and 'I find that the amount expended for the protection of the fisheries throughout the province of Ntew Brunswick up to the end of the fiscal year 1915 amounted to $59,709.06. I turn to the report for the fiscal year 1912, and I find that for the same service in the province of New Brunswick the total amount was $42,708.01, or an advance in three years of $117,151.65, or over forty per cent.' I notice that the number of officers, is about the same. Increases of salary and expenses, I suppose, go to make up the difference, but it does seem to me that it is a pretty large increase in three years for the same service, in the same territory. As I have said, I have no fault to find with the officials who are engaged; I simply draw the minister's attention to the fact that the	increase in
the expenditure has been very marked, indeed, in that section of the province. I want to draw the minister's attention to the fact that fishermen, particularly lobster fishermen, this coming season, are going to be put in a very difficult position by reason of the very great increase in the
price of gasolene and rope. As my hon. friend knows, all the lobster fishermen down in that locality, and, I suppose in every locality now, use gasolene boats for setting and tending their traps. I am informed that gasolene was sold to the fishermen last year at 194 cents per gallon by the barrel and that this year it will be something like 33 or 34 cents per gallon.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: More than that.

It will be before they commence fishing, but I believe it is being sold now for 33 or 34 cents per gallon by the cask. Rope, I understand, was selling for something like 13 cents a pound and it is now selling for 19 cents. These are two commodities of the very greatest importance to fishermen in preparing and setting their nets and traps .and in using their boats. Unless something is done to assist the fishermen in this regard, it will be almost impossible to get men who will be able to go out and carry on the lobster industry during the coming season. It may be impossible for the department to give any assistance, I do not know if anything can be done along that line, but if anything can be done, it would be very much appreciated by the fishermen.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My hon. friend has. spoken about the price of gasolene. There is no doubt that it is going to be very much higher in price and it is going to be a serious matter for fishermen who use gasolene in thefr boats not only in connection with the lobster fishery but every other fishery as well. But, the prospects are that the price of lobsters will be very much advanced and that will assist the fishermen in meeting this increased expense. There is no duty on gasolene coming into this country.
There is a duty of 74 per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
That is the only duty on gasolene but that is only a small part of the price. I do not know what can be done in the matter nor do I know what suggestion my hon. friend has to offer. A certain addition to the price of gasolene has been caused by the war, but I fancy that the tremendously increased number of motors, vehicles, and boats, all over this country is having its effect. I saw some figures the other day of the increase in the number of automobiles in Canada and the. United States and they were

simply astonishing. This creates a very much greater demand for gasolene. I presume that before long, when they get an engine that is adapted to it, kerosene will be used for motive power. The present prospects are that the lobster fishermen will receive a very much higher price for their catch during the coming year and this increased price may put them in as good a position as they were in before, even if they have to pay more for their gasoline than they did last year. Before the season is over the price of gasolene will probably be double' what it was last year.
Henry Ford is experimenting on something to take the place of gasolene.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.

I want to draw the
minister's attention to a matter that I have discussed with him on two other occasions in the last three or four years. The reason I am doing so at this late hour is that I have to go away to-morrow and I may not have another opportunity. I refer to the condition of affairs on the St. John river and its tributaries. Without referring to Hansard, I think it was in the session of 1913 that I called his attention to the fact that the regulation, and the law, regarding salmon fishing on the St. John were being violated, not only violated by the people but by his guardians. I went so far as to give him the name of one of his guardians in my own constituency who was well known to be a violator of the law. My hon. friend promised me that he would investigate this matter and see that this man was removed from office unless there was a change. He will remember that either on that occasion, or a few days afterwards-I think it was a few days afterwards-we had a private conversation in the presence of a couple of his. fishery officers in which the statement made was substantiated. That man is still the fishery guardian there, or was last year and the year before.
Under the regulations on the St. John river, from the head of tide water, some distance above Fredericton, I think at Andover bridge, the people are allowed to fish for salmon during two consecutive weeks, followed by a close season of two weeks, with nets of a certain sized mesh and of certain dimensions. It is believed-in fact I make the statement-that nets of different sizes, not at all complying with the regulations, are being used and the result is that the fish that ought to go up the Tobique river

for spawning purposes are becoming so scarce that it has become a very grave question whether the salmon will be entirely depleted. It is a fact that the
11 p.m. Tobique river is the only spawning ground for-the whole of the St. John Waters. I made a trip through part of the Tobique river country last summer and also the summer before, and I made it my business to inquire of the people along that river as to what they thought about it. It may surprise the minister when I tell him that I was informed that about 500 people are relying on the fishing industry, or the industry that comes there as a result of the fishery, for their living. These are men who are engaged as guides or in looking after tourists and people of that class. They tell me that the fish on the Tobique river are becoming depleted to such an extent that men are ceasing to go there. They believe it is all because the fish are being swept out of the river. It is almost impossible for a salmon to get past the hundreds (of nets which they have to face from the head of tide water up to Andover bridge. I do not want to make charges against any person, because I have given my hon. friend the name of one of the guardians. I told him that there	was another one
about which I	thought I could
make the same statement, but with-. out having positive proof I did not feel like mentioning his name, although I gave it to the minister privately. But I did not have the same proof in that case as I had in the case of the man whose name I mentioned. There is nothing I know of in that portion of the county of Victoria that is of greater importance than this. It does not play so much of a part in my own constituency. That is a constituency in which they allow netting to take place. Of course, there are a great many people who would like to go out, set a net and catch a salmon. But that is only an incident. Our people are farmers although they like to get a salmon now and then. Unless something is done to /lessen the evil, I see nothing for it but to ask the department to entirely cancel the regulations. I know that would be very distasteful to many people.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The regulation allowing
two weeks of fishing?
Yes. I think it would be far better to cancel the regulations entirely than allow them to be violated with the result that the source of the supply of fish is going to be entirely depleted.

What would be the good of that if the officer was no good?
' Mr. CARVHLL:	The difficulty is this:
where the regulations .permit fishing for two weeks at a time the people get their nets ready and go on fishing for four weeks. That is what it amounts to. The officers of the department are not doing their duty. I do not want to mention names, but I could tell the minister of men in my constituency who are drawing their pay, but who spend hardly ten hours out of the week on the Tiver; they are following their ordinary vocations, and do not possess a boat; I doubt whether some of them know how to stand up in a boat. The whole thing is one great farce, and it is becoming a real detriment to the district at large, because the American sportsmen who come there to fish and hunt are practically the whole livelihood of very many people. I was told last summer, on a trip up the Tobique river, that at least 500 people make their living catering to these American sportsmen. I do not need to elaborate on this, for the minister knows the district as well as I do. He knows the St. John river well enough to know that practically every stream from the mouth up to the Tobique river is dammed, and that the Tobique river is practically the only one in which the salmon are spawning.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Unless they are spawning in the main river.

They may be, but I
doubt it. In.a season such as 1912 it did not make very much difference, as the river was full of water and the fish could get around, the nets; but in a season like 1914, when the river was very low, it was almost a physical impossibility for the salmon to get up the St. John river as far as the Tobique. I do not want to. say anything unpleasant, but I do wish the minister would give this matter some consideration and get rid of the absolutely useless wardens he has got, and appoint men who would enforce the law. I had a good deal to do with the passing of the .regulation before 1911. At that time there were about half a dozen men in Carleton county who had always fished and they said they were going to fish right (along, no matter what regulations were passed. We told them that they were not going to fish, and we laid information against them and stopped them. One man was a good Conservative, and a friend of mine. After he was prosecuted he was convinced that he had been breaking the law, and I do not think he has ever violated it since. My hon. friend knows that the Tobique Salmon Club have tried to enforce the regulations. I know they have come to the minister personally, and sent him letters, if not petitions, protesting against the violation of the law. They have gone .so far as to send their own wardens up the river to make investigations, and have seized nets in some cases, though I have always doubted their authority to do so; in fact, in some cases they have been compelled to give them back. But they cannot do much because they lack authority. They tell me, and I know they have told the minister that the law is being violated in dozens and dozens of places, and they have given the minister the names of the offenders, and the names of the wardens who are not doing their duty. ' So the minister has a pretty intimate knowledge of the condition, of affairs, and I am just bringing the matter to his attention now in the hope that he will try and have the law enforced more strictly in the future. If he cannot get any honest Conservatives in Carleton. and York counties to .act as wardens and enforce the law, I will try and find him a few bad Grits; I should not have to take the best Grits, the poorest ones would enforce the. law.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: As has been said by my hon. friend, fishing is not allowed in the St. John river above the head of the tide, which is- at Crook's point.
My hon. friend must have changed it. It is a good many miles further up the river.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It has not been changed since we came into power. That is where it was in 1911, and no fishing was allowed above that. About 1908 or 1910 an arrangement was made whereby the people along the river could catch a salmon now and then. They thought it was a hardship if they could not catch an occasional salmon, so they were allowed to fish for two weeks, then there was a close season of two weeks, and then another two weeks' fishing.
I think the regulations provide that even in the two weeks fishing the nets must be taken up from Saturday night until Monday morning.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
That is the general law. My information is to the effect that the salmon in the St. John river, and in the

waters into which the St. John river flows, are increasing year by year. This is largely due to artificial propagation, perhaps to a better enforcement of the law than in years gone by, and, in a measure, to the extra protection the salmon are getting from the Tobique Salmon Club, which controls the Tobique river. The Tobique river is practically the only river to which salmon now resort for spawning. I am told, though, that of late years they are getting up the Kennebecasis river as far as Sussex. The mills on that river had been removed, and no saw-dust was getting into the water. It is claimed by certain fishery officers that the salmon also spawn at certain places in the St. John river. There is a pool above Fredericton, called Hartt's Pool, where many salmon are caught. It is also claimed that the salmon are spawning above Woodstock. That may or may not be the case, but there is no doubt that more salmon are being caught along the St. John river to-day than in years gone by. The Tobique Salmon Club, which controls the Tobique river, is composed mainly of American gentlemen living in Washington, New York, and other large cities in the United States. They spend a large sum of money on the river yearly. They protect it very carefully against poaching, and they protect the fish on the spawning beds.
My hon. friend states that there are 500 people working for these sportsmen including hunters, and there ist no doubt the fishing on the river is a very important industry to that part of the country. When the pools ware first leased by the provincial Government there was great indignation among the people on account of their being deprived of their industry, because they could not fish, while the wealthy people could fish as they could afford to lease the pools. That feeling has changed very largely on account of the fact that those wealthy people spend a large amount of money, employ guides, and so on, and the result has been very much to the benefit of the community. From the Tobique river up to the county of Carleton I have had no complaint, and I have had no complaints in the county of York. There have been some complaints regarding conditions in the county of Carle-ton, and I have had personal interviews with gentlemen representing the Tobique Salmon Club. They did not give the names of any'violators of the law; they did not tell me of the law being violated dozens and dozens of times, which I think is the expression used by my hon. friend; but they

mentioned to me the names of two officers who, they said were not doing their duty. I have been having the matter inquired into and it will be rectified, but that wras the only charge made to me by these gentlemen, so that my hon. friend has been given an erroneous account of the assertions made. The impression I got was that the condition of affairs generally was satisfactory; that they thought it would have been better if there had not been that previous grant of two weeks' fishing which was granted out of deference to the sentiment of people along the river and with which I have no fault to find, because I think if the law is enforced and there are two weeks fishing granted, the result will be there will be lots of salmon in the Tobique river for those who are spending money to catch them for sport, and also for the purpose of propagation, so that there will be plenty of salmon going up and down the river in the season. Those people, some months ago, came to me and I have taken steps now with a view of having their complaints remedied. No complaint has reached me about anything in the county of York or above Carleton, and I think that agrees with what my hon. friend has said. I am not questioning the bona fides of my hon. friend; I believe he has stated what has been stated to him, but the statements which he has -made are not the same as the statements made to me by the members of the Tobique Salmon Club.

I take my hon, friend's word for the statements made to him, and I want to say quite frankly that I hold no -brief at all for the Tobique Salmon Club. In fact, all the business I have ever had with them has been to start law suits against them, and I have had quite an experience along that line.
Did you win them?

I did. I have, however, had a number of conversations with the manager and many of his guides, and I am very much surprised at the moderation with which they must have approached the minister, because it was in quite a different attitude that they approached me. I am giving my opinion, obtained not so much from the Tobique Salmon Club, as from the people along the Tobique river. It is quite true, as my hon. friend -says, that many years ago, when the province of New Brunswick leased the fishing rights, their action was very bitterly opposed by
r

the people. In fact, I think murder was committed as a result of it. But in talking over the matter with the people along the river, as I have done for the last two years, I have never heard a solitary comment by any resident along that river against protecting the fish. On the contrary, it is all in favour of protecting the fish. The people have come to the conclusion that they are making much more money through protecting the fish than they would make otherwise, and; all the complaints I hear-and they are many

are against the Government for not protecting the fish. They feel that the fish in the Tobique river are protected, they find no complaint in regard to that, and I have never heard of any complaint along the St. John river in the county of Victoria, that is, a, distance of only nine or ten miles from the Andover bridge, but the fault is, as my hon. friend has stated, in the county of Carleton. While the people may haye complained of only two of the wardens as .being_ guilty of malfeasance, there must be 'a great deal of complaint of at least negligence on the part of most of the wardens. It may be that my hon. friend has not duly impressed upon those wardens the fact that they are supposed to give some little return foT the money they receive. It looks to me as though they have not been properly instructed, because from my certain knowledge, men whom I know as well as I know my hon. friend the minister-and I have had quit^ a long acquaintance with him-men who live so near me that I have an opportunity of knowing what they are doing-	.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
An inspector is sent personally to instruct them.
Mr. CARViELL: Well those men are not spending their time on the river and yet they are drawing their money for guarding the river. Their work is simply a sinecure. There are wardens in the county of Carleton, who, I believe, are not spending one day in the week on the river. How much are they paid a day?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: $1.50 a day for the days they work.,
Their diaries will show that they work seven days a week.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
They have to make an affidavit as to their work and also to go before the inspector. Of course, they may
be conspiring together. I do not know, but I do not think that is the case.

I do not think they are conspiring, but they have been taught that this is only a little reward for their services. I do not think those men believe they are perjuring themselves because, with the exception of one, they are responsible men, I am sure they would not perjure themselves willingly, and I do not think they would want practically to steal money from the Government. That, however, does not get around the fact that they are giving simply no value for the money they are receiving. The minister should take this matter out of the hands of those who are advising him in the matter; he could find men who Will advise him properly and put men on that work who will do their duty and see that the fish are protected. I may get some little adverse comment on account of what I am saying to-night, because there are many men in the county of Carleton who like to catch fish out of the river, but I am telling the minister the honest truth, and if he will enforce the law and protect the fish, the people in the county of Carleton can get all the fish they are entitled to, the fish will have a chance to go up the river to their spawning grounds and the great industry at the mouth of the river will not be ruined as it otherwise will be.
I understand from what the minister states that the fish are going up the Kennebecasis river as far as- Sussex, but the St. John river is liable to great fluctuations of rise and fall; and as the fish spawn in the months of September and October, often the water is so high that spawning is almost impossible. I hope the minister will, give this matter a little more attention than he has given it in the past and that he will forget the question of politics. Of course, I expect him to appoint Conserva- -tives, but let him appoint Conservatives who will enforce the law and see that the work is properly done, and I do not think he will have any complaint from me in the future.
Progress reported.
On motion of Mr. Hazen for the adjournment of the House:

Can the hon. minister
(Mr. Hazen) tell me what business we are to take up to-morrow? And can he give us any information as to when the discussion on the resolution of the right hon. leader

of the Opposition will be resumed? Has any arrangement been made?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No arrangement had been made between the leader of the Opposition and the Prime Minister when I last saw the Prime Minister late this afternoon. I can not give my hon. friend any information on that point. Tomorrow, I presume, we will take up whatever Bills are on the Order Paper, and then go into Supply, taking up the Estimates of Fisheries, Interior, and Public Works, or one of these.

I may not have the
privilege of being here for a couple of days, and, as I have a very strong sense of fairness, I wanted to make this suggestion before I went away. The discussion on the resolution of the leader of the Opposition will probably, as it has done in the last few days, concern the Minister of Militia (Sir Sam Hughes), and as it is announced that he is leaving for home, I think it but fair that that gentleman should have an opportunity on the floor of the House to make a statement concerning matters that have been discussed in his absence. No matter what our views may be, the Minister of Militia is a member of this House and one of our colleagues, and I believe that, in justice to him-and it would be no injustice to anybody else-the debate should not be closed until he has had an opportunity to make a statement concerning the matters discussed in his absence.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I will call the attention of the Prime Minister to my hon. friend's views.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion agreed to, and the House adjourned at 11.40 p.m.
Friday, March 31, 1916.
